{{Politics of Austria}}

[[General election|Legislative elections]] were held in [[Austria]] on 29 September 2024 to elect the 28th [[National Council (Austria)|National Council]], the lower house of Austria's bicameral parliament.

The election saw the far-right [[Freedom Party of Austria]] (FPÖ) place first, winning 28.8% of the vote and achieving the best result in the party's history. This was the first time that a [[far-right party]] won the most seats in a legislative election in Austria after World War II.<ref name="Karnitschnig 2024">{{cite news |last=Karnitschnig |first=Matthew |title=Austria goes back to the future as voters embrace far-right party founded by Nazis |url=https://www.politico.eu/article/austria-far-right-freedom-party-win-national-election-early-projections-herbet-kickl/ |newspaper=Politico |department=Europe |date=2024-09-29}}</ref><ref name="Australian Broadcasting Corporation 2024">{{cite news |title=Austria's Freedom Party secures first national election win for far-right since World War II |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-09-30/austria-far-right-first-election-win-since-second-world-war/104412948 |publisher=Australian Broadcasting Corporation |department= |date=2024-09-30}}</ref><ref name="Harris 2024">{{cite news |last=Harris |first=Rob  |title=Austrian far-right party wins first national election since World War II |url=https://www.smh.com.au/world/europe/austria-s-first-far-right-national-election-win-since-world-war-2-20240930-p5kefv.html |newspaper=The Sydney Morning Herald |department=World elections |date=2024-09-30}}</ref> As a result, the FPÖ, for the first time in its history, was able to occupy the position of the [[President of the National Council (Austria)|President of the National Council]] ([[Walter Rosenkranz]]) but ultimately fell short of participating in the government. The governing [[Austrian People's Party]] (ÖVP) lost 20 seats, while its coalition partner, the [[The Greens (Austria)|Greens]], lost 10 seats. The centre-left [[Social Democratic Party of Austria|Social Democratic Party]] (SPÖ) won just 21.1%, marking its worst result ever in terms of percentages and the place occupied (3rd), but it gained one seat compared to the previous election. [[NEOS (Austria)|NEOS]] slightly improved from 2019, rising from 15 to 18 seats. No other party was able to clear the 4% threshold to win seats.

==Background==
The [[2019 Austrian legislative election|2019 legislative election]] was called after the [[Ibiza affair]], which triggered the collapse of the [[coalition government]] between the [[Austrian People's Party]] (ÖVP) and the [[Freedom Party of Austria]] (FPÖ) led by Chancellor [[Sebastian Kurz]]. The coalition was ousted in a [[motion of no confidence]] and replaced by a non-partisan interim government.<ref>{{cite web |title=Austrian parliament topples Chancellor Sebastian Kurz |url=https://www.dw.com/en/austrian-parliament-topples-chancellor-sebastian-kurz/a-48904760 |website=[[Deutsche Welle]] |date=27 May 2019}}</ref> The election delivered a strong victory for the ÖVP, which rose to 37.5%, while the FPÖ declined to 16%, its worst result since 2008. With 21%, the opposition [[Social Democratic Party of Austria]] (SPÖ) recorded its worst performance in over a century. [[The Greens (Austria)|The Greens]] returned to the National Council after failing to win seats in 2017, achieving its best-ever result with 14%. [[NEOS (Austria)|NEOS]] improved to 8%.<ref>{{cite web |title=Austria's far right loses ground as Sebastian Kurz wins landslide |url=https://www.dw.com/en/austrias-far-right-loses-ground-as-sebastian-kurz-wins-landslide/a-50633489 |website=[[Deutsche Welle]] |date=30 September 2019}}</ref>

The ÖVP formed a coalition with The Greens, a first on the federal level in Austria. The new government took office in January 2020, with Sebastian Kurz returning as Chancellor.<ref>{{cite web |title=Austria: Greens enter government for first time, join Kurz's conservatives |url=https://www.dw.com/en/austria-greens-enter-government-for-first-time-join-kurzs-conservatives/a-51853261 |website=[[Deutsche Welle]] |date=1 January 2020}}</ref>

[[Norbert Hofer]] announced his resignation as leader of the Freedom Party in June 2021. He was replaced by parliamentary group leader [[Herbert Kickl]], whose dismissal as interior minister caused the collapse of the ÖVP–FPÖ government in 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dw.com/en/austria-herbert-kickl-elected-to-lead-far-right-freedom-party/a-57971160|title=Austria: Herbert Kickl elected to lead far-right Freedom Party|date=20 June 2021|website=[[Deutsche Welle]]}}</ref>

On 6 October 2021 agents of the Central Prosecutorial Agency for Corruption and Economic Affairs (WKStA) raided the Federal Chancellery and the headquarters of the ÖVP as part of a [[Kurz corruption probe|corruption probe]] targeting Chancellor Sebastian Kurz and his "inner circle". Prosecutors alleged that, in 2016, Kurz paid bribes to news outlets to publish coverage and opinion polling favourable to himself, the goal of the scheme being to undermine then-ÖVP leader [[Reinhold Mitterlehner]] so that Kurz could take his place.<ref>{{cite web |title=Austrian prosecutors target Kurz in bribery investigation |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/prosecutors-raid-austrian-conservatives-hq-fresh-headache-kurz-2021-10-06/ |publisher=[[Reuters]] |date=7 October 2021}}</ref> The Greens threatened to support a [[motion of no confidence]] if Kurz did not step down as Chancellor. He thus announced his resignation on 9 October and was replaced by Foreign Minister [[Alexander Schallenberg]]. However, he was quickly elected faction leader of the ÖVP in the National Council; it was widely understood that he would remain ''de facto'' leader of the government.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dw.com/en/austrian-chancellor-sebastian-kurz-announces-resignation/a-59458714|title=Austrian Chancellor Sebastian Kurz announces resignation|date=9 October 2021|website=[[Deutsche Welle]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dw.com/en/alexander-schallenberg-sworn-in-as-chancellor-of-austria/a-59469255|title=Alexander Schallenberg sworn in as chancellor of Austria|date=11 October 2021|website=[[Deutsche Welle]]}}</ref>

On 2 December, Kurz announced he would resign from all offices and retire from politics, citing a desire to focus on his family after becoming a father. Shortly after, Schallenberg announced he would resign as Chancellor in favour of the new ÖVP leader once one had been elected.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dw.com/en/austrian-chancellor-resigns-after-sebastian-kurz-withdraws-from-politics/a-59993547|title=Austrian chancellor resigns after Sebastian Kurz withdraws from politics|date=2 December 2021|website=[[Deutsche Welle]]}}</ref> On 3 December, Interior Minister [[Karl Nehammer]] was unanimously appointed as leader of the ÖVP by the federal party committee and proposed as Chancellor.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dw.com/en/austria-karl-nehammer-set-to-become-new-chancellor/a-60006966|title=Austria: Karl Nehammer set to become new chancellor|date=3 December 2021|website=[[Deutsche Welle]]}}</ref> He was sworn in by President [[Alexander Van der Bellen]] on 6 December.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dw.com/en/austria-karl-nehammer-sworn-in-as-new-chancellor/a-60032938|title=Austria: Karl Nehammer sworn in as new chancellor|date=6 December 2021|website=[[Deutsche Welle]]}}</ref>

Since 2019 numerous new and old minor parties such as [[Team HC Strache – Alliance for Austria]], [[MFG Austria – People Freedom Fundamental Rights]], [[The Beer Party (Austria)|The Beer Party]] and the [[Communist Party of Austria]] received at times considerable support in the [[2020 Viennese state election]], [[2021 Upper Austrian state election]], [[2022 Austrian presidential election]], [[2023 Salzburg state election]] and various local elections, allowing these parties to win seats.

During the first year of the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Austria|COVID-19 pandemic]], the ÖVP-Green government enjoyed high support. The government then became deeply unpopular after it passed a mandatory vaccination law, which led to a strong polarization of the population. As a result, and because of large-scale public protests, the mandatory vaccination law (one of few in the world) was later dropped and was never enforced.{{citation needed|date=September 2024}}

After a series of corruption scandals involving the ÖVP and rising [[inflation]] – such as skyrocketing housing, electricity, fuel and grocery prices – the government parties lost considerable support in 4 subsequent state elections in [[2022 Tyrolean state election|Tyrol]], [[2023 Lower Austrian state election|Lower Austria]], [[2023 Carinthian state election|Carinthia]] and [[2023 Salzburg state election|Salzburg]]. As of May 2023, inflation in Austria was still around 10% and continues to be much higher than the [[Eurozone]] average, at around 7%.{{citation needed|date=September 2024}}

Under Nehammer's leadership, Austria's government implemented a package of measures worth six billion euros ($6.3 billion){{As of?|date=September 2024}} in 2022 aimed at cushioning the blow to households of the rising cost of living.<ref>Francois Murphy (14 June 2022), [https://www.reuters.com/markets/europe/austria-announces-6-bln-euro-package-address-cost-of-living-crisis-2022-06-14 "Austria announces 6 billion euro package to address cost-of-living crisis"], [[Reuters]].</ref> The measures helped limit poverty, but according to experts increased inflation further.{{citation needed|date=September 2024}}

On 8 December 2022, Nehammer was the architect of blocking [[Romania]] and [[Bulgaria]]'s access into the [[Schengen Area]]. Nehammer said he first wants the EU to introduce strict border controls at the EU's outer border to limit illegal immigration before the two countries should be allowed to join Schengen.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.thelocal.at/20221208/austria-vetoes-bulgaria-and-romania-joining-europes-schengen-area/|date=8 December 2022|title= Austria vetoes Bulgaria and Romania joining Europe's Schengen area|website=[[The Local]]}}</ref>

On 3 June 2023, after years of internal conflicts, intrigues and crossfire, the opposition SPÖ [[2023 Social Democratic Party of Austria leadership election|elected]] a new party leader. The non-binding party membership vote ahead of the binding party congress was won by [[Hans Peter Doskozil]], although by a simple plurality of votes, leaving the door open for a challenge by second-place finisher [[Andreas Babler]] at the party congress. On 23 May 2023, incumbent party leader [[Pamela Rendi-Wagner]] announced that she would not be a candidate at the party congress, after coming in just third in the membership vote and announced her orderly resignation. On 25 May 2023, Rendi-Wagner announced her complete withdrawal from Austrian politics by the end of June, also resigning as a member of the Austrian Parliament. On 3 June 2023, Hans Peter Doskozil was elected as the new party chairman with 53% of the delegates. However, two days later the SPÖ announced that the results had been mixed up in [[Microsoft Excel]] spreadsheets and that Babler was the actual winner with 53%, thus becoming the new party chairman.<ref>{{cite web |title=Austria's SPÖ party announces Babler as leader after vote mix-up |url=https://www.thelocal.at/20230605/breaking-austrias-spo-party-announces-babler-as-leader-after-vote-mix-up |website=[[The Local]] |date=5 June 2023}}</ref>

The turmoil experienced by both the governing coalition and the SPÖ allowed FPÖ to top the polls during 2023, positioning it to win an Austrian legislative election for the first time.<ref>{{Cite web |title=General Elections 2024 Austria |url=https://www.robert-schuman.eu/en/monitor/6304-the-far-right-leads-the-polls-for-the-austrian-federal-elections-on-29-september |access-date=2025-08-07 |website=www.robert-schuman.eu |language=fr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2024-09-30 |title=Austria's far right achieves highest election result since 1945 |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2024/09/30/austria-s-far-right-achieves-highest-election-result-since-1945_6727747_4.html |access-date=2025-08-07 |language=en}}</ref>

According to polls conducted in May 2023, a government led by the FPÖ with Herbert Kickl as Chancellor was opposed by about two in three Austrians. Additionally, President [[Alexander Van der Bellen]] said that he might not swear in a FPÖ-led government with Kickl as Chancellor, but that he remains open to swearing in a more moderate FPÖ Chancellor.{{citation needed|date=September 2024}}

The rise in inflation and in particular the increasingly unaffordable cost of housing saw the [[Communist Party of Austria]] (KPÖ) rise considerably in opinion polls conducted before the legislative election. The party received a record 11.7% percent of the vote in the [[2023 Salzburg state election]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=2023-04-24 |title=Austrian communist party stages major comeback |url=https://www.euractiv.com/section/politics/news/austrian-communist-party-stages-major-comeback/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240602082251/https://www.euractiv.com/section/politics/news/austrian-communist-party-stages-major-comeback/ |archive-date=2024-06-02 |access-date=2025-08-07 |work=www.euractiv.com |language=en-GB}}</ref>

On 18 August 2023, Kurz (ÖVP) was charged in federal court for allegedly making false statements to a parliamentary investigation committee.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-08-18 |title=Former Austrian leader Kurz charged with giving false evidence to a corruption inquiry |url=https://apnews.com/article/austria-sebastian-kurz-charged-former-chancellor-7a9e3ba0f9f2d7e3a9827967d1cb5ba2 |access-date=2025-08-07 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref>

On 11 November 2023, the new SPÖ leader Andreas Babler was confirmed at a party convention in Graz by 89 percent of voting delegates.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://orf.at/stories/3339497/|date=11 November 2023|title=SPÖ-Parteitag: 88,76 Prozent für Babler als Parteichef|website=[[ORF (broadcaster)|orf]].at}}</ref>

On 18 January 2024, Dominik Wlazny (alias [[Marco Pogo]]) announced the candidacy of the [[The Beer Party (Austria)|Beer Party]] (BIER).<ref>{{cite web |author=Florian Amelin |date=2024-01-18 |title=ANTRETEN BEI NATIONALRATSWAHL: "Günstige Gemengelage" für Bierpartei |url=https://orf.at/stories/3346049/ |access-date=2024-01-18 |website=news.ORF.at |language=de}}</ref>

===Date===
The election had to be held before the conclusion of the five-year term of the 27th National Council on 23 October 2024 (typically, regularly scheduled elections are held several weeks earlier than that, to allow for the publication of an official certified election result). Elections are traditionally not held during the school summer holidays, from early July to mid-September.{{citation needed|date=September 2024}}

Due to the government's unpopularity, it was often speculated in the media that early elections would be called for the spring of 2024, but the ÖVP-Green government repeatedly said it wanted to finish its term and that the election would be held in September 2024.<ref>{{cite web|title=Warum Neuwahlen immer unwahrscheinlicher werden|url=https://kurier.at/politik/inland/neuwahlen-unwahrscheinlich-nehammer-kogler-oevp-gruene-fpoe/402650006|publisher=Kurier.at|date=30 October 2023|access-date=11 November 2023}}</ref>

In February 2024, Minister of Agriculture [[Norbert Totschnig]] (ÖVP) mentioned that the election would likely be held on Sunday 29 September 2024, exactly five years after the previous election.{{citation needed|date=September 2024}}

On 28 June 2024, the federal government formally announced the election date of 29 September 2024.<ref>{{cite web|title=Verordnung der Bundesregierung über die Ausschreibung der Wahl zum Nationalrat, die Festsetzung des Wahltages und des Stichtages (BGBl. II 169/2024)|url=https://www.ris.bka.gv.at/Dokumente/BgblAuth/BGBLA_2024_II_169/BGBLA_2024_II_169.pdfsig|publisher=ris.bka.gv.at|date=28 June 2024|access-date=4 July 2024}}</ref> Polling stations opened at 07:00 and closed at 17:00.<ref name="auto">{{cite web |title=Austrians vote in tight legislative election as far right eyes unprecedented win |url=https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20240929-austrians-vote-in-tight-election-as-far-right-eyes-unprecedented-win |access-date=2024-09-29 |website=France 24 |date=29 September 2024}}</ref>

==Electoral system==
[[File:Wien - Parlamentsgebäude.JPG|200px|thumb|Austrian Parliament in Vienna (2023)]]
The 183 members of the [[National Council (Austria)|National Council]] are elected by [[open list]] [[proportional representation]] at three levels; a single national constituency, nine constituencies based on the [[states of Austria|federal states]], and 39 regional constituencies. Seats are apportioned to the regional constituencies based on the results of the most recent census. For parties to receive any representation in the National Council, they must either win at least one seat in a constituency directly, or clear a 4 percent national [[electoral threshold]].<ref name="system-1">{{cite web|title=Wahlen zum Nationalrat|url=https://www.parlament.gv.at/PERK/PARL/DEM/NRWAHL/|publisher=Österreichisches Parlament|date=12 September 2017|access-date=28 October 2017}}</ref>

Following the elections, seats are allocated to the candidates of successful parties and lists in a three-stage process, starting with the regional constituencies. Seats are distributed according to the [[Hare quota]] in the regional constituencies, and with unallocated seats distributed at the state constituency level.<ref>{{cite web|title=Wahlen|url=http://www.bmi.gv.at/412/|publisher=Bundesministerium für Inneres|access-date=28 October 2017}}</ref> Any remaining seats are then allocated using the [[D'Hondt method]] at the federal level, to ensure overall proportionality between a party's national vote share and its share of parliamentary seats.<ref>{{cite web|title=Das Verhältniswahlrecht und das Ermittlungsverfahren bei der Nationalratswahl|url=https://www.parlament.gv.at/PERK/FAQ/WAHL/ERMNRWAHL/index.shtml|publisher=Österreichisches Parlament|date=21 October 2017|access-date=28 October 2017}}</ref>

In addition to voting for a political party, voters may cast three preferential votes for specific candidates of that party, but are not required to do so.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.oesterreich.gv.at/themen/leben_in_oesterreich/wahlen/1/Seite.320260.html|title=Vorzugsstimmenvergabe bei einer Nationalratswahl|website=State of Austria (official website)|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=16 October 2019}}</ref> These additional votes do not affect the proportional allocation based on the vote for the party or list, but can change the rank order of candidates on a party's lists at the federal, state, and regional level. The threshold to increase the position of a candidate on a federal party list is 7 percent, compared to 10 percent at the state level, and 14 percent at the regional level. The names of candidates on regional party lists are printed on the ballot and can be marked with an "x" to indicate the voter's preference. Preference votes for candidates on party lists at the state and federal level, however, must be written in by the voter, either by writing the name or the rank number of the candidate in a blank spot provided for that purpose.<ref>{{cite web|title=Vorzugsstimmenvergabe bei einer Nationalratswahl|url=https://www.help.gv.at/Portal.Node/hlpd/public/content/32/Seite.320260.html|publisher=HELP.gv.at|date=1 January 2017|access-date=28 October 2017}}</ref>

===Voting law reform===
The ÖVP–Green government decided in early 2023 to reform the voting law. Among the reforms were the introduction of an early voting period, beginning three weeks before election day, during which voters can request absentee ballots in every municipality. Voters can either fill out the ballot in the municipality and therefore cast the ballot early, or take the absentee ballot with them and cast it later by mail, or in-person before or on election day. Previously, this was only possible in large cities. Another reform will be the counting of almost all absentee and mail-ballots on election day. Previously, most mail ballots were counted on the Monday and Thursday after election day. The new changes would lead to most votes being counted on election day, while only a much smaller number of late-arriving mail ballots and mail ballots from electoral districts other than the voters' own district will be counted on the Monday after election day. The [[2024 European Parliament election in Austria]] was the first national election in which the new law took effect, and it showed that only about 130,000 absentee ballots had to be counted on the Monday after election day, compared to almost 960,000 on the Monday after the 2019 legislative election. Other reforms include measures to lower the number of invalid or spoilt votes among absentee/mail ballots, by re-designing mail ballot instructions and introduction of "easy language" (or [[plain language]]) on them. High fines and a prison sentence of up to two weeks will be introduced for election commission members who deliberately leak election results of their polling stations to the media or other third parties before poll closing time. The reform of the voting law, which took effect on 1 January 2024, was also supported by the three opposition parties SPÖ, FPÖ and NEOS, after several amendments were made to satisfy these parties too. The reformed election law<ref>{{cite web|title=Wahlrechtsänderungsgesetz 2023 (3002/A)|url=https://www.parlament.gv.at/gegenstand/XXVII/A/3002|publisher=Österreichisches Parlament (Austrian Parliament)|date=22 November 2022|access-date=5 November 2023}}</ref> was approved by the Nationalrat (National Council) on 31 January 2023 and by the Bundesrat ([[Federal Council (Austria)|Federal Council]]) on 16 February 2023.<ref>{{cite web|title=PARLAMENTSKORRESPONDENZ NR. 91 VOM 31.01.2023: Nationalrat gibt grünes Licht für Wahlrechtsreform - Gesetzespaket erhielt nach weiterer Adaptierung einhellige Zustimmung|url=https://www.parlament.gv.at/aktuelles/pk/jahr_2023/pk0091|publisher=Österreichisches Parlament (Austrian Parliament)|date=31 January 2023|access-date=5 November 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Wahlrecht wird reformiert – was sich alles ändert|url=https://gemeindebund.at/wahlrecht-wird-reformiert-was-sich-alles-aendert/|publisher=Österreichischer Gemeindebund (Austrian Association of Municipalities)|date=21 November 2022|access-date=5 November 2023}}</ref>

==Statistics==
According to final numbers from the Federal Ministry of the Interior, a total of 6,346,059 people were eligible to vote in the election. In the 2019 election, 6,396,812 people were eligible to vote, so the number of eligible voters fell by 50,753 people. This is because the number of Austrian citizens has been falling for years due to a birth deficit and negative migration balance to abroad, which is not compensated for by the number of naturalizations. The final number of eligible voters was published on 27 September 2024 after a period for objections and the correction of the electoral rolls.<ref name=MOIeligible>[https://www.bmi.gv.at/412/Nationalratswahlen/Nationalratswahl_2024/files/endgueltige_wahlberechtigte_NRW24_BF_27092024.pdf Comparison of the final number of eligible voters in the National Council election on 29 September 2024 with the final number of eligible voters in the National Council election on 29 September 2019], Federal Ministry of the Interior, on 27 September 2024</ref>

Absentee/mail ballots were sent to voters who requested them, starting 2 September 2024. Early voting in every municipality was also possible from that day, by immediately casting absentee ballots there (after requesting them at the municipal election department).{{Citation needed|date=September 2024}}

Electoral authorities all over Austria issued a total of 1,436,240 absentee ballots by 27 September 2024, the last day to request one. This is a new record and much higher than the 1,070,933 issued for the 2019 election. In total, about 23% of all eligible voters requested an absentee ballot, compared to 17% in 2019. The [[Ministry of the Interior (Austria)|Ministry of the Interior]] projected that every fourth vote cast in this election would be absentee.<ref name=MOIeligible />

==Contesting parties==
Any party that intends to be on the ballot for the election must submit a statement of candidacy, its candidate list, a filing fee of €435 and either the signatures of three members of the Austrian National Council, or sufficient petition signatures of eligible Austrian voters by 1 August 2024 at 17:00 at the federal election commission in the Austrian Interior Ministry. To be on the ballot in all nine states, 2,600 signatures are required, with individual states requiring between 100 and 500 signatures. Parties contesting the election in only some states only need to reach the signature threshold for those states.

==Campaign==
All major parties started their election campaigns in mid-to-late August 2024. First waves of election billboards and campaign posters were placed at heavily frequented places and roads, lead candidates appeared in TV interviews and discussions and ads on social media, radio and TV were launched. Each party can spend a maximum of 8.6 million euros for the election, in accordance with campaign finance laws.{{citation needed|date=September 2024}}

Especially after the [[2024 Vienna terrorism plot]] in early August 2024, in which the [[Islamic State]] unsuccessfully tried to target concerts of the American singer-songwriter [[Taylor Swift]], the campaigning shifted heavily towards security and policing issues, how to tackle political and extremist [[Islam in Austria]] and on immigration and the integration of (primarily Muslim) immigrants in Austria.<ref>{{cite web |last=Matzl |first=Christoph |date=2024-08-25 |title=Stricter rules on immigration called for |url=https://www.krone.at/3503571 |access-date=2024-09-26 |website=Kronen Zeitung}}</ref> The focus on these topics were reinforced by the [[2024 Solingen stabbing]] in late August 2024 in neighboring Germany, with the FPÖ calling for "zero asylum" in Austria, increased deportations of criminal foreigners to their home countries and a new law to ban [[Islamism|political/extremist Islam]] in Austria, similar to [[Verbotsgesetz 1947|Austria's anti-Nazi law]]<ref>{{cite web |date=2024-08-23 |title=FPÖ vows to curb migration and abolish 'green taxes' |url=https://brusselssignal.eu/2024/08/austrias-fpo-vows-to-curb-migration-abolish-green-taxes-upon-election-win/ |access-date=2024-09-26 |website=Brussels Signal |language=en-GB}}</ref> in its campaign program titled "Fortress Austria".<ref name="fortress">{{cite web |date=2024-09-30 |title=Austria's Freedom Party secures first far-right national election win since World War II |url=https://apnews.com/article/austria-national-election-far-right-freedom-party-1a22057b230a2576e0ca0ee69607cf6e |access-date=2024-09-29 |website=Associated Press|language=en-US}}</ref> The FPÖ also called for enshrining legal recognitions of binary genders in the constitution,<ref>{{cite web |date=2024-09-29 |title=Is Austria's far right poised for historic win in Sunday elections? |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/9/28/is-austrias-far-right-poised-for-historic-win-in-sunday-elections |access-date=2024-09-29 |website=Al Jazeera |language=en-US}}</ref> restoring some political powers from the [[European Union]] to Austria,<ref name="fortress"/> ending [[sanctions against Russia]] and Austria's exit from the [[European Sky Shield Initiative]]. The FPÖ also heavily emphasised [[remigration]], particularly to Islamic countries, during its campaign.<ref>{{cite news|work=MSN|title=Leidende FPÖ zet bij Oostenrijkse verkiezingen in op remigratie|date=21 August 2024|url=https://www.msn.com/nl-be/nieuws/politiek/leidende-fp%C3%B6-zet-bij-oostenrijkse-verkiezingen-in-op-remigratie/ar-AA1pbj84?ocid=BingNewsVerp}}</ref>

The SPÖ and the ÖVP both attacked Herbert Kickl, with its leaders describing him as "a threat to democracy" and a "security risk". Both parties pledged not to join a government led by the FPÖ, although Karl Nehammer has not ruled out forming a coalition with the FPÖ that would exclude Kickl from the cabinet.<ref>{{cite web |date=2024-09-29 |title=Austrians vote as a far-right party hopes for its first national election win |url=https://apnews.com/article/austria-national-election-far-right-freedom-party-1a22057b230a2576e0ca0ee69607cf6e |access-date=2024-09-29 |website=Associated Press|language=en-US}}</ref>

The FPÖ's use of the term ''Volkskanzler'' (People's Chancellor) to describe Kickl in its campaign material has caused criticism among some Austrians for its usage by [[Adolf Hitler]] in the 1930s and as a reminder of the FPÖ's origins as a party founded by former Nazis in the 1950s.<ref>{{cite web |date=2024-09-28 |title=Austria's far right eyes unprecedented election win |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cr4xz013zx7o |access-date=2024-09-28 |publisher=[[BBC News]] |language=en-GB}}</ref>

The ÖVP campaigned on a platform of stability.<ref>{{cite web |title=Austria votes in general election as far right eyes victory |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/9/29/austria-votes-in-general-election-as-far-right-eyes-victory |access-date=2024-09-29 |website=Al Jazeera}}</ref> It also pledged to implement tighter immigration laws and tax cuts.<ref name="auto"/>

==Aftermath==
Celebrations broke out among FPÖ supporters after initial projections showed them winning a plurality of votes. FPÖ general secretary [[Michael Schnedlitz]] said "the men and women of Austria have made history today", while [[Herbert Kickl]] called on other parties to reconsider forming a coalition with his party. In response, Karl Nehammer reiterated that the ÖVP would not enter into a coalition with the FPÖ unless Kickl was excluded from a ministerial position.<ref>{{cite web |title=Far right in Austria set for election victory - projections |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c8rdygy5888o |publisher=BBC News |access-date=29 September 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Austria's far-right Freedom Party projected to win election |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/9/29/austrias-far-right-freedom-party-projected-to-win-election |publisher=Al Jazeera |access-date=29 September 2024}}</ref> Nehammer also said he was "bitter" over the ÖVP failing to win but acknowledged his role in improving the party's showing following low opinion ratings.<ref name="fortress"/>

A protest was held outside the [[Austrian Parliament Building]] in Vienna by around 300 people protesting against Kickl on 29 September, calling him a "Nazi".<ref name="fortress"/> The leaders of far-right parties across Europe, including Hungarian Prime Minister [[Viktor Orbán]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.politico.eu/article/far-right-across-europe-celebrates-victory-austria-freedom-party-herbert-kickl-anti-immigration/|title=Orbán, Le Pen and Wilders are buzzing over Austria's far right winning election|author= Csongor Körömi |date=September 30, 2024|work=www.politico.eu|access-date=15 October 2024}}</ref> [[Marine Le Pen]] of the [[National Rally]] in France,<ref>{{cite web |title=Far right in Austria 'opens new era' with election victory |date=30 September 2024 |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c8rdygy5888o |publisher=BBC News |access-date=30 September 2024}}</ref> [[Matteo Salvini]] of the [[Lega (political party)|League]] in Italy,<ref>[https://www.ilfoglio.it/politica/2024/09/30/news/salvini-esulta-per-la-vittoria-di-fpo-in-austria-ma-tajani-respingere-i-rigurgiti-neonazisti--6996074/ Salvini esulta per la vittoria di Fpo in Austria. Ma Tajani: "Respingere i rigurgiti neonazisti"]. Il Foglio</ref> [[Santiago Abascal]] of [[Vox (political party)|Vox]] in Spain,<ref>{{cite web |date=2024-09-30 |title=Abascal celebra la victoria de FPÖ en Austria |url=https://electomania.es/abascal-celebra-la-victoria-del-partido-de-la-libertad-fpo-en-austria/ |access-date=2024-09-30 |website=Electomanía |language=es}}</ref> [[Geert Wilders]] of the [[Party for Freedom]] in the Netherlands, and [[Alice Weidel]] of the [[Alternative for Germany]], sent congratulations to Kickl and the FPÖ.<ref name="fortress" />

In the first poll after the election, Market-Lazarsfeld for Ö24 found that the FPÖ was supported by 30%, the ÖVP by 25%, the SPÖ by 20%, NEOS by 11%, the Green Party by 8%, and others by 6% of voters. A plurality of voters preferred a coalition by FPÖ-ÖVP (29%), followed by ÖVP-SPÖ-NEOS (23%), ÖVP-SPÖ-Greens (12%), ÖVP-SPÖ (9%), FPÖ-SPÖ (9%), other coalitions (3%), and 15% undecided.<ref>{{cite web |title=Umfrage: Bei Neuwahl könnt FPÖ 30-%-Marke knacken |url=https://www.oe24.at/oesterreich/politik/nationalratswahl/umfrage-bei-neuwahl-koennt-fpoe-30-marke-knacken/608263286 |work=oe24.at |date=4 October 2024 |access-date=4 October 2024}}</ref> Another new poll after the election by Unique Research for Heute found that 58% of Austrians want the Austrian president to officially task the FPÖ with forming the next government, while 36% were opposed. Among FPÖ voters, 98% were in favour, among ÖVP voters the support was at 54%, and 44% were opposed. Among all other party voters, opposition outweighed support.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wahl-Knaller: Mehrheit will, dass Kickl Regierung sucht |url=https://www.heute.at/s/wahl-knaller-mehrheit-will-dass-kickl-regierung-sucht-120064986 |work=heute.at |access-date=4 October 2024}}</ref>

===Government formation===

President [[Alexander Van der Bellen]] pledged to ensure the formation of a government that respects the "foundations of our [[liberal democracy]]".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Austria far-right supporters toast historic victory |url=https://www.france24.com/en/live-news/20240930-austria-far-right-supporters-toast-historic-victory |work=France 24 |date=30 September 2024 |access-date=30 September 2024}}</ref> Although it is a [[Convention (political norm)|convention]] that the president first asks the leader of the largest party to try to form a government, the [[Constitution of Austria|constitution]] does not require them to do so.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Murphy |first1=Francois |title=Austria's president takes charge as far right isolated after election victory |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/austrias-president-takes-charge-far-right-isolated-after-election-victory-2024-09-30/ |work=Reuters |date=30 September 2024}}</ref> Van der Bellen previously stated that he might not give FPÖ this mandate in the event of their victory.<ref>{{cite news |title=Gespräche bei Van der Bellen: Kickl macht den Anfang |url=https://orf.at/stories/3371816/ |work=news.ORF.at |date=3 October 2024 |language=de}}</ref> On 2 October, the outgoing ÖVP-Green government tendered its resignation, although it was asked to stay on in a caretaker role by Van der Bellen. The president then started official talks with all party leaders on 4 October, with FPÖ leader Kickl being the first to talk with the president. Van der Bellen and Kickl made no statements after their meeting but Kickl said he would do so on 5 October.<ref>{{cite web |title=Regierung mit Fortführung betraut |url=https://orf.at/stories/3371674/ |work=ORF.at |date=2 October 2024 |access-date=2 October 2024}}</ref> Nehammer and other ÖVP governors expressed support for the FPÖ receiving the first mandate to form a government, citing a wish to preserve the convention.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Murphy |first1=Francois |title=Austria's conservatives want far right to be asked to form coalition |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/austrias-conservatives-want-far-right-be-tasked-with-forming-coalition-2024-10-01/ |work=Reuters |date=1 October 2024}}</ref>

The president spoke on 7 October with Nehammer (ÖVP) and Babler (SPÖ)—who also met with each other the next day—and on 8 October with Meinl-Reisinger (NEOS) and Kogler (Greens).<ref>{{cite news |title=Medien: ÖVP und SPÖ reden miteinander am Dienstag |url=https://orf.at/stories/3371943/ |work=news.ORF.at |date=5 October 2024 |language=de}}</ref> Babler had previously ruled out a coalition government with ÖVP,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Oltermann |first=Philip |date=2023-06-05 |title=Austrian Social Democrats announce wrong leader after 'technical error' |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/jun/05/austrian-social-democrats-announce-wrong-leader-after-technical-error |access-date=2025-04-16 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077 |quote=Unlike Doskozil, Babler has ruled out forming a “grand coalition” with Austria’s conservatives.}}</ref> but backtracked.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Andreas Babler Has Disappointed the Austrian Left |url=https://jacobin.com/2024/12/austria-babler-spo-left-right |access-date=2025-04-16 |website=jacobin.com |language=en-US}}</ref> After these initial talks with each party leader, Van der Bellen said he asked the party leaders to "sort things out on their own" until 18 October rather than tasking the FPÖ with the mandate to form the next government. Van der Bellen said that the situation is unique in the sense that no other party wants to cooperate with the FPÖ and that it would be ludicrous to order the FPÖ to form a government in this situation. Instead, Van der Bellen ordered the parties to keep talking with each other until a credible path to a government appears, after which he would task the leading party of this constellation to form the next government. Meanwhile, the FPÖ rose to a new high of 33% in [[Next Austrian legislative election#Opinion polls|a new Market-Lazarsfeld poll for Ö24]], with the ÖVP holding at 26% and the SPÖ falling slightly to 19% (below 20% for the first time); the minor parties held fairly steady: NEOS at 10%, the Green Party at 7%, KPÖ at 2%, and others at 3%.<ref>{{cite news |title=NACH DER WAHL: Regierungsbildung als Präzedenzfall |url=https://orf.at/stories/3372386/ |work=news.ORF.at |date=10 October 2024 |language=de}}</ref>

After the FPÖ–ÖVP–SPÖ talks concluded on 16 October, Nehammer reiterated his opposition to a government with Kickl, who insisted to lead the next government himself as Chancellor. Nehammer said "Kickl is unable to govern," adding that he was a "security threat for the country" and that "Nehammer and the ÖVP are not willing to be the stirrup holders of Kickl and the FPÖ." On the other hand, Kickl called Nehammer "an offended and aggrieved sore loser, whose main goal is to continue clinging to power, but without the interests of the country and voters in mind."<ref>{{cite news |title=KICKL: Nehammer "beleidigter Wahlverlierer" |url=https://orf.at/stories/3372962/ |work=news.ORF.at |date=16 October 2024 |language=de}}</ref>

On 22 October, Van der Bellen officially asked Nehammer to form the next government and negotiate with the SPÖ.<ref>{{cite news |title=Austria's chancellor asked to form new government after parties refuse to work with far-right leader |url=https://apnews.com/article/austria-president-nehammer-chancellor-government-far-right-b7c91e9030d266d92f348f52acd9e5a8 |work=Associated Press |date=22 October 2024}}</ref> Van der Bellen said that it was clear that Kickl "would not be able to find a coalition partner who would make him Chancellor," while Kickl criticised Van der Bellen for breaking with the "tried and tested normal processes" of asking the leading party in the election to form a government and pledged, "Today is not the end of the story."<ref>{{cite news |title=Austria far right shunned for coalition despite winning election |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cx252kedeppo |publisher=BBC News |date=22 October 2024}}</ref> Nehammer said that he would need to find a third coalition partner to ensure a stable parliamentary majority. An ÖVP–SPÖ coalition would only have a majority of one seat in the National Council, which would be impractical for daily government work, as any member would have the power to block proceedings.

On 25 October, Nehammer and the ÖVP officially launched first exploration talks with Babler and the SPÖ. Nehammer also talked with NEOS and Green delegations to try to find a third coalition partner. After the talks, Nehammer said that the "road to a new government will be long and stony" because of the "massive policy differences between the parties involved."<ref>{{cite news |title=DREIERKOALITION: NEOS mit besseren Chancen als Grüne |url=https://orf.at/stories/3373886/ |work=news.ORF.at |date=25 October 2024 |language=de}}</ref>

==== Failed ÖVP-SPÖ-NEOS coalition negotiations ====
On 12 November, the centre-right [[Austrian People's Party|ÖVP]] and the center-left [[Social Democratic Party of Austria|SPÖ]] announced they would start coalition talks with the liberal [[NEOS (Austria)|NEOS]].<ref>{{cite news |title=SONDIERUNGEN: ÖVP und SPÖ laden NEOS ein |url=https://orf.at/stories/3375755/ |work=news.ORF.at |date=12 November 2024 |language=de}}</ref> The talks started on 18 November.<ref>{{cite web |date=2024-11-18 |title=Startschuss für Verhandlungen über eine Koalition ÖVP – SPÖ – NEOS |url=https://www.trend.at/politik/startschuss-fuer-koalitionsverhandlungen-zwischen-oevp-spoe-und-neos |access-date=2024-11-18 |website=trend.at |language=de}}</ref>

On 3 January 2025, various Austrian media outlets reported that NEOS had withdrawn from coalition talks, leaving it unclear how government negotiations would move forward. It was reported that the [[The Greens (Austria)|Green Party]] could be asked to join negotiations or that negotiations between only the FPÖ and ÖVP or FPÖ and SPÖ could start instead. Alternatively, new elections could be called.<ref>{{cite news |title=NEOS dürfte aus Koalitionsverhandlungen austreten |url=https://orf.at/stories/3380629/ |work=news.ORF.at |date=3 January 2025 |language=de}}</ref>

On 4 January, after consultations with President Van der Bellen, ÖVP and SPÖ continued coalition talks without any other party.<ref>{{cite news |title=ÖVP und SPÖ verhandeln wieder |url=https://orf.at/stories/3380737/ |work=news.ORF.at |date=4 January 2025 |language=de}}</ref> However, Nehammer resigned as chancellor and ÖVP leader later that same day after concluding that no agreement was possible.<ref name="resigned">{{cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2025-01-04/austrian-chancellor-nehammer-steps-down-as-coalition-talks-fail|title=Austrian Chancellor Nehammer Steps Down as Coalition Talks Fail |accessdate=4 January 2025|website=[[Bloomberg News]]}}</ref>

Nehammer was replaced by [[Christian Stocker]] as interim ÖVP leader the same day, and his resignation as chancellor took effect on 10 January. When asked why he was resigning before then, he said only it was a step he did not want to take. In a statement, Nehammer said his ultimate goal was to keep Kickl out of the chancellor's office "because I have always been of the opinion that his understanding of the office [and] the way he lives politics is not good for our country", though there were "many reasons" why he failed.<ref>{{cite news |title=Nehammer wird am Freitag als Kanzler zurücktreten |url=https://orf.at/stories/3381038/ |work=news.ORF.at |date=6 January 2025 |language=de}}</ref>

[[File:Wien - Demo gegen FPÖ-Regierungsbeteiligung, 9. Jän. 2025 (b).JPG|thumb|Demonstration against FPÖ participation in government in front of the [[Federal Chancellery of Austria|Federal Chancellery]] on January 9, 2025 in Vienna]]

==== Failed FPÖ-ÖVP coalition negotiations ====
On 6 January, President Van der Bellen formally tasked [[Freedom Party of Austria|FPÖ]] leader [[Herbert Kickl]] to form a government.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/1/6/austrian-president-tasks-far-right-leader-with-forming-government | title=Austrian president tasks far-right leader with forming government }}</ref> The coalition talks continued through February, with no reported breakthrough.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-01-31 |title=Koalitionsverhandlungen laufen weiter |url=https://www.vienna.at/koalitionsverhandlungen-auch-am-wochenende/9191671 |access-date=2025-02-01 |website=vienna.at}}</ref> The FPÖ and ÖVP negotiated for over a month about forming a new government.

The FPÖ advocated for substantial tax cuts, increased public borrowing and reduced contributions to EU-wide financial mechanisms. These policies clashed with the ÖVP, which remained committed to fiscal discipline and adherence to [[European Union|EU]] economic frameworks.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-02-27 |title=Far right gets shut out as Austrian government forms |url=https://www.politico.eu/article/austria-coalition-forms-prevents-far-right-power/ |access-date=2025-03-04 |website=POLITICO |language=en-GB}}</ref> Additionally, the FPÖ's Russia-friendly stance and [[Euroscepticism|Eurosceptic]] views clashed with the ÖVP's pro-European and pro-NATO alignment.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Henley |first=Jon |date=2025-02-27 |title=Austrian centrist parties reach deal to form government without far right |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/feb/27/austria-centrist-parties-deal-form-government-without-far-right |access-date=2025-03-04 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

On 12 February, Kickl announced after a meeting with President Alexander Van der Bellen in Vienna that the negotiations had failed. The parties had argued primarily about the distribution of ministries, because both sides wanted to take over the [[Ministry of the Interior (Austria)|Ministry of the Interior]] and the [[Ministry of Finance (Austria)|Ministry of Finance]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Koalitionsgespräche von FPÖ und ÖVP in Österreich gescheitert |url=https://www.tagesschau.de/ausland/europa/oesterreich-koalitionsverhandlungen-gescheitert-102.html |access-date=2025-02-12 |website=Tagesschau |language=de}}</ref> According to [[Christian Stocker]], the ÖVP wanted to retain control over the finance and interior ministries to secure a “defensible constitutional state” and ensure cooperation with international intelligence services.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-02-12 |title=Austria's political crisis deepens as far right pulls plug on coalition talks |url=https://www.politico.eu/article/austria-coalition-talks-collapse-far-right-herbert-kickl-freedom-party-fpo-peoples-party-ovp/ |access-date=2025-03-04 |website=POLITICO |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Sattler |first1=Armin |last2=Bauer |first2=Patrick |last3=Lenzer |first3=Florian Zischkaund Harald |last4=ORF.at |first4=alle |date=2025-02-10 |title=Kickl für "rasche Neuwahlen" |url=https://orf.at/live/5463-Kickl-fuer-rasche-Neuwahlen-/#e40317 |access-date=2025-03-04 |website=news.ORF.at |language=de}}</ref>

==== Successful ÖVP-SPÖ-NEOS coalition negotiations ====

On 22 February, after a week of exploration talks, the three parties informed President Van der Bellen that they would try to create a joint government again. The negotiations were already in its final stages, because most topics had already been agreed on during their previous failed negotiations and even some measures from the FPÖ-ÖVP negotiations, such as the planned budget consolidation for 2025, were likely to be adopted.<ref>{{cite news |title=ÖVP, SPÖ, NEOS: Verhandlungen "auf der Zielgeraden" |url=https://orf.at/stories/3385594/ |work=news.ORF.at |date=22 February 2025 |language=de}}</ref>

On 27 February, the leaders of the three parties announced that they had come to a coalition agreement. The agreement was subjected to a vote of NEOS party members on 2 March, passing with 94% of the vote.<ref>{{cite news |title=Austria: Centrist parties form coalition without far-right |url=https://www.dw.com/en/austria-centrist-parties-form-coalition-without-far-right/a-71765298 |work=dw.com/en |date=2 March 2025 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2 March 2025 |title=Austrian liberals' vote removes last obstacle to coalition government|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/austrian-liberals-hold-party-vote-crucial-future-coalition-government-2025-03-02/|access-date=2 March 2025 |work=[[Reuters]]}}</ref> The coalition will have 110 deputies, greater than the 92 needed for a majority.

On 3 March, President [[Alexander Van der Bellen|Van der Bellen]] officially swore in the new [[Stocker government|three-party coalition government]]. [[Christian Stocker]] of the ÖVP took office as Chancellor, while [[Andreas Babler]] of the SPÖ was appointed Vice Chancellor, and [[Beate Meinl-Reisinger]] of NEOS assumed the role of Foreign Minister.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Liveticker-Nachlese: Österreich hat eine neue Bundesregierung |url=https://www.derstandard.at/consent/tcf/jetzt/livebericht/3000000259591/angelobung-live-neue-regierung-abbei-van-der-bellen?ref=live_red_content&responsive=false |access-date=2025-03-04 |website=DER STANDARD |language=de-AT}}</ref> In his remarks, Van der Bellen praised the coalition for putting the national interest above party divisions, stating, "Good things come to those who wait."<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-03-03 |title=Austria swears in new government, ending five-month political crisis |url=https://www.politico.eu/article/austria-swears-new-government-ending-five-month-political-crisis-christian-stocker-alexander-van-der-bellen/ |access-date=2025-03-04 |website=POLITICO |language=en-GB}}</ref>

election]] was held on 21 May 2022 to elect members of the [[47th Parliament of Australia]]. The incumbent [[Morrison government|Liberal–National Coalition government]], led by Prime Minister [[Scott Morrison]], sought to win a fourth consecutive term in office but was defeated by the [[Australian Labor Party|Labor Party]], led by Opposition Leader [[Anthony Albanese]]. Up for election were all 151 seats in the [[lower house]], the [[Australian House of Representatives|House of Representatives]], as well as 40 of the 76 seats in the [[upper house]], the [[Australian Senate|Senate]]. The voter turnout of 89.82% in this election was the lowest in modern history, falling below 90% for the first time since [[1922 Australian federal election|1922]], prior to the introduction of [[compulsory voting in Australia]]. The Labor Party achieved a [[majority government]] for the first time since 2007, winning 77 seats in the House of Representatives. Albanese was sworn in as Prime Minister on 23 May 2022, becoming the fourth Labor leader to win government from opposition since [[World War II]], after [[Gough Whitlam]] in [[1972 Australian federal election|1972]], [[Bob Hawke]] in [[1983 Australian federal election|1983]], and [[Kevin Rudd]] in [[2007 Australian federal election|2007]].{{cite news|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-05-23/anthony-albanese-sworn-in-as-31st-prime-minister/13894004|title=Video: Anthony Albanese sworn in as 31st Prime Minister of Australia|publisher=Australia Broadcasting Corporation|date=23 May 2022|access-date=23 May 2022}} Every state and territory except [[Tasmania]] swung to Labor on a [[Two-party-preferred vote|two-party-preferred basis]]. The largest two-party preferred swing was in [[Western Australia]] (10.6%), where Labor won a majority of seats for the first time since [[1990 Australian federal election|1990]]. The Coalition suffered severe losses, winning 58 seats, its lowest share in the House of Representatives since [[1946 Australian federal election|1946]], the first federal election contested by the [[Liberal Party of Australia|Liberal Party]].{{cite news |last=Curtis |first=Katina |title=Liberals at lowest proportion of seats since party's first poll in 1946 |url=https://www.smh.com.au/politics/federal/liberals-at-lowest-proportion-of-seats-since-party-s-first-poll-in-1946-20220524-p5ao00.html |access-date=25 May 2022 |newspaper=The Sydney Morning Herald |date=24 May 2022}} On election night, Morrison conceded defeat and announced he would resign as Liberal leader,{{Cite web |last=McGuirk |first=Rod |date=2022-05-21 |title=Australia's prime minister concedes defeat after election results; Labor Party wins election |url=https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/story/2022-05-21/election-results-suggest-opposition-party-more-likely-to-form-australias-government |access-date=2023-08-07 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}} and was subsequently replaced by [[Peter Dutton]].{{cite web |last1=Hitch |first1=Georgia |date=30 May 2022 |title=Peter Dutton elected new Liberal Party leader, Sussan Ley becomes deputy leader |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-05-30/peter-dutton-liberal-party-leader-sussan-ley-deputy/101109498 |access-date=22 June 2022 |website=ABC News |publisher=}} While [[Coalition (Australia)|the Coalition]] was soundly defeated, Labor did not achieve a [[landslide victory]], as a result of electoral successes by [[Independent politicians in Australia|independent]] candidates and the [[Australian Greens|Greens]], with the [[crossbench]] swelling to 16 seats. Six formerly safe Liberal seats in urban and suburban areas, most held by the party and its predecessors for decades, were won by [[teal independents]], unseating Liberal incumbents including Treasurer and Deputy Liberal Leader [[Josh Frydenberg]]. The Liberals also suffered large swings in a number of suburban seats that had long been reckoned as Liberal heartland. The Greens increased their vote share and won four seats, gaining three seats in inner-city [[Brisbane]], the first time in the party's history it won more than one seat in the lower house. The combined major party vote for Labor and the Coalition was the lowest on record at 68.3%, while the minor party and independent vote was at its highest at 31.7%.{{cite news |last1=Nicholas |first1=Josh |last2=Evershed |first2=Nick |date=28 May 2022 |title=Votes for Labor and the Coalition plummet to all-time low as Australia swings away from major parties |newspaper=[[The Guardian]] |location=London |url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/datablog/2022/may/28/votes-for-labor-and-the-coalition-plummet-to-all-time-low-as-australia-swings-away-from-major-parties |access-date=2022-06-01 |issn=0261-3077}} Compared to 2019, Labor's primary vote dropped much less than the Coalition's, although Labor nevertheless recorded its lowest primary vote since either [[1903 Australian federal election|1903]] or [[1934 Australian federal election|1934]], depending on whether the [[Lang Labor]] vote is included.{{cite news |date=4 July 2022 |title=Barnaby Joyce says Labor's 2022 primary vote was its lowest since 1910. Is that correct? |work=ABC News |publisher= |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-07-05/fact-check-barnaby-joyce-labor-primary-vote/101129054 |access-date=5 July 2022}} In the [[Australian Senate|Senate]], Labor won 15 seats and retained its 26 seats overall in the chamber, while the Coalition fell to 32 seats, a four-seat drop from the previous parliament. The Greens won a seat in every state, an increase of 3 for a total of 12 seats overall, the party's largest ever representation in the Senate. One Nation returned its leader [[Pauline Hanson]] in Queensland to retain 2 seats overall, while the [[Jacqui Lambie Network]] won an additional seat in Tasmania to have 2 seats. In the [[Australian Capital Territory]] (ACT), independent candidate [[David Pocock]] won the second of two seats, the first time an ACT senator was not a Labor or Liberal party member. Lastly, [[Ralph Babet]] of the [[United Australia Party (2013)|United Australia Party]] won the sixth seat in Victoria. Labor required 13 votes from a crossbench of 18 (including 12 Greens) to ensure passage of legislation not supported by the Coalition.{{cite web|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/elections/federal/2022/results/senate|title=Senate Results|work=ABC News|date=21 May 2022|access-date=2 June 2022}}{{cite web |author=Butler |first=Josh |date=20 June 2022 |title=Labor steady, Coalition down, crossbench up: who's who in the new Senate |url=https://theguardian.com/australia-news/2022/jun/20/labor-steady-coalition-down-crossbench-up-whos-who-in-the-new-senate |work=The Guardian}} ==Background== ===Previous election=== {{main|2019 Australian federal election}} {{see also|Results of the 2019 Australian federal election (House of Representatives)}} {{see also|Results of the 2019 Australian federal election (Senate)}} At the previous election in May 2019, the [[Liberal–National Coalition]], led by [[Scott Morrison]], formed a government after winning 77 seats in the House of Representatives, enough for a three-seat majority, whilst Labor claimed 68 seats and remained in [[Opposition (Australia)|opposition]]. A further six seats were won by other parties and [[Independent politicians in Australia|independents]], one each to the [[Australian Greens|Greens]], [[Centre Alliance]], and [[Katter's Australian Party]], and the remaining three by independents forming the [[Crossbencher|crossbench]]. In the Senate, the Coalition made modest gains in most states and increased their share of seats to 35 overall, whilst Labor remained steady on 26, the Greens likewise on 9, [[Pauline Hanson's One Nation|One Nation]] and Centre Alliance down to 2 each, and [[Jacqui Lambie]] and [[Cory Bernardi]]'s minor parties with 1 seat each. This meant the Coalition required four additional votes to pass legislation.{{cite web |last=Muller |first=Damon |title=The 2019 federal election |url=https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp1920/2019FederalElection |publisher=Australian Parliamentary Library |access-date=10 April 2022 |archive-date=10 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220410221507/https://www.aph.gov.au/About_Parliament/Parliamentary_Departments/Parliamentary_Library/pubs/rp/rp1920/2019FederalElection |url-status=live}} ===Composition of parliament=== {{see also|46th Parliament of Australia#Membership changes}} The [[46th Parliament of Australia|46th Parliament]] was inaugurated on 2 July 2019. By this time, the Labor Party had elected a new leader, replacing the outgoing [[Bill Shorten]] with [[Anthony Albanese]].{{cite news |last=Yosufzai |first=Rashida |title=Bill Shorten will step down as Labor leader after election defeat |url=https://www.sbs.com.au/news/bill-shorten-will-step-down-as-labor-leader-after-election-defeat |date=1 May 2019 |website=SBS News}}{{cite news |last=Worthington |first=Brett |date=27 May 2019 |title=Anthony Albanese to become Labor's new leader unopposed following shock federal election loss |work=ABC News |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2019-05-27/anthony-albanese-the-new-labor-leader-following-election-loss/11152036?section=politics}} In the Senate, [[Cory Bernardi]]'s resignation in January 2020 allowed the Coalition to replace him with a [[Liberal Party of Australia|Liberal]] member, increasing their share of seats in the Senate to 36.{{cite news |last=Bonyhady |first=Nick |title=Conservative senator Cory Bernardi resigns from Parliament |url=https://www.smh.com.au/politics/federal/conservative-senator-cory-bernardi-resigns-from-parliament-20200120-p53t08.html |access-date=21 April 2022 |work=The Sydney Morning Herald |date=20 January 2020 |archive-date=21 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220421221929/https://www.smh.com.au/politics/federal/conservative-senator-cory-bernardi-resigns-from-parliament-20200120-p53t08.html |url-status=live}} They retained this figure until [[Northern Territory]] senator [[Sam McMahon]] resigned from the [[Country Liberal Party]] in January 2022, four months before the election. She joined the [[Liberal Democratic Party (Australia)|Liberal Democratic Party]] on 8 April 2022.{{cite news |date=8 April 2022 |title=NT politician Sam McMahon joins ex-Queensland premier's party to run for re-election |work=ABC News |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-04-08/sam-mcmahon-announces-federal-senate-election-bid-nt/100975390 |access-date=8 April 2022 |archive-date=11 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220411113907/https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-04-08/sam-mcmahon-announces-federal-senate-election-bid-nt/100975390 |url-status=live|author=Garrick, Matt}} In the House of Representatives, two Coalition MPs ([[Llew O'Brien]] and [[Darren Chester]]) departed their respective party-room caucuses, though retained their membership of the Morrison government.{{cite web |last=Harris |first=Rob |date=26 September 2021 |title=Chester's departure might be least of Joyce's troubles right now |url=https://www.smh.com.au/politics/federal/chester-s-departure-might-be-least-of-joyce-s-troubles-right-now-20210926-p58uvg.html |access-date=22 May 2022 |website=The Sydney Morning Herald |publisher=}} The government's share of seats in the House dropped when [[Craig Kelly]], the member for [[Division of Hughes|Hughes]], left the Liberal Party in August 2021 to become an independent and sit on the crossbench.{{cite web |last=Murphy |first=Katharine |date=23 February 2021 |title=Craig Kelly quits Liberal party to move to the crossbench |url=https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2021/feb/23/craig-kelly-quits-liberal-party-to-move-to-the-crossbench |access-date=22 May 2022 |work=The Guardian}} This left the government with a one-seat majority (76 out of 151), though considering the position of the [[Speaker of the Australian House of Representatives|Speaker]], who is obliged not to vote to create a majority where none is present, the government functioned from this point to the election in technical-minority status. On 7 April 2022, three days prior to the election being called, [[Liberal National Party of Queensland|Liberal National Party]] MP [[George Christensen]] announced his resignation from the party and became an independent, dropping the government to 75 seats at the end of the parliamentary term.{{cite news |last=Doran |first=Matthew |date=19 January 2022 |title=George Christensen steps down as chair of parliamentary committee after controversial COVID-19 vaccine comments |work=ABC News |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-01-19/george-christensen-resigns-chair-committee-covid-vaccine-comment/100767918 |access-date=22 May 2022}} There were two [[by-elections]] in the 46th parliament, both in 2020 in the seats of [[2020 Eden-Monaro by-election|Eden-Monaro]] and [[2020 Groom by-election|Groom]]; in both instances, the by-elections were won by the incumbent party.{{cite Spence|Spence]] as it would be too close to the federal election. ===Events of the 46th Parliament=== Throughout the duration of the 46th Parliament, [[Scott Morrison]] remained Prime Minister and Changes to party registration rules were reportedly the effect of an increase of parties on the Senate ballot, which resulted in the requirement of magnifying sheets for some voters to read the ballot, and a perception that voters would be misled by names of some minor parties. The first change was the increase of membership requirements for a party from 500 to 1,500.{{cite news |title=Changes to federal election rules including party sizes and names pass Parliament |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2021-08-26/federal-election-rule-change-party-size-name-pass-parliament/100410134 |last=Lowrey |first=Tom |access-date=5 January 2022 |work=ABC News |date=26 August 2021 |archive-date=5 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220105101844/https://www.abc.net.au/news/2021-08-26/federal-election-rule-change-party-size-name-pass-parliament/100410134 |url-status=live }}{{cite web|url=https://www.aec.gov.au/Parties_and_Representatives/Party_Registration/guide/index.htm|title=Electoral Legislation Amendment (Party Registration Integrity) Act 2021 (Party Registration Act)|website=Australian Electoral Commission|access-date=22 March 2022|archive-date=28 March 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220328170346/https://www.aec.gov.au/Parties_and_Representatives/Party_Registration/guide/index.htm|url-status=live}} This resulted in the federal deregistration of non-parliamentary minor parties who could not prove they had at least 1,500 members, including the [[Christian Democratic Party (Australia)|Christian Democratic Party]] and [[Democratic Labour Party (Australia, 1980)|Democratic Labour Party]] in March 2022.{{cite web|url=https://www.aec.gov.au/parties_and_representatives/Party_Registration/Deregistered_parties/index.htm|title=Deregistered political parties|website=Australian Electoral Commission|access-date=22 March 2022|archive-date=22 March 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220322031621/https://www.aec.gov.au/parties_and_representatives/Party_Registration/Deregistered_parties/index.htm|url-status=live}} The second change was that parties cannot have names that were too similar to political parties registered before them. This meant that new parties are prevented from registering a party name or logo "too similar to an existing party's". As for existing registered parties, a party may also object to a similar name or logo used by another party, if the latter party was registered later than the former party. If the [[Australian Electoral Commission]] (AEC) is satisfied with the objection, it can uphold the objection, and the later-registered party will be registered within a month of the upholding, if an application to change the name or logo is not made or has been denied.{{cite web|url=https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/legislation/bills/r6755_aspassed/toc_pdf/21101b01.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf|title=Electoral Legislation Amendment (Party Registration Integrity) Bill 2021 – As passed by both Houses|website=Parliament of Australia|access-date=22 March 2022|archive-date=28 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210828094922/https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/legislation/bills/r6755_aspassed/toc_pdf/21101b01.pdf;fileType=application/pdf|url-status=live}} This "similar name" rule was used by the [[Liberal Party of Australia|Liberal Party]] against the [[Liberal Democratic Party (Australia)|Liberal Democratic Party]] (LDP) and [[The New Liberals]], with both objections upheld by the AEC. ===Party preselection issues=== {{see also|Victorian Labor Party|New South Wales Liberal Party}} Both the Labor Party and Liberal Party experienced preselection issues, where they were unable to finalise candidates for many of the seats or the Senate as late as early April 2022, less than two weeks before the election was called. This resulted in the intervention by the parties' national executives or nominated committees to select the candidates and bypassing local voting by rank-and-file members. The New South Wales state division of the Liberal Party was unable to finalise candidates for many seats by March 2022 due to the alleged failure of Morrison's representative [[Alex Hawke]] to attend internal Liberal Party nomination review committee meetings and COVID-19 complications resulting in the inability to elect the state executive in November 2020.{{cite news |last=Cockburn |first=Paige |date=24 February 2022 |title=Court asked to rule in long-running Liberal Party power struggle over who gets to choose candidates in NSW seats |work=ABC News |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-02-24/nsw-liberal-party-pre-selection-court-stoush/100857000 |url-status=live |access-date=29 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220330023355/https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-02-24/nsw-liberal-party-pre-selection-court-stoush/100857000 |archive-date=30 March 2022}} This had forced the federal executive of the party to temporarily dissolve the state executive on two occasions (4 to 8 March, and 27 March to 2 April) under the party constitution, and set up a committee to intervene in preselection processes. The committee was made up of Morrison, New South Wales [[Premier of New South Wales|Premier]] and Liberal leader [[Dominic Perrottet]] and former party president [[Chris McDiven]].{{cite web |last=Osborne |first=Paul |date=4 March 2022 |title=Federal Liberals step in over NSW stoush |url=https://7news.com.au/politics/federal-liberals-weigh-up-nsw-candidates-c-5923144 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220328080347/https://7news.com.au/politics/federal-liberals-weigh-up-nsw-candidates-c-5923144 |archive-date=28 March 2022 |access-date=29 March 2022 |website=7News |publisher=}}{{cite news |last1=Cockburn |first1=Gerard |last2=Barlow |first2=Karen |date=4 March 2022 |title=Federal arm of Liberal Party takes over NSW branch for not complying with preselection rules |newspaper=The Canberra Times |url=https://www.canberratimes.com.au/story/7645072/pm-takes-joint-control-of-nsw-liberals-can-choose-candidates/?cs=14264 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription |access-date=29 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220328080336/https://www.canberratimes.com.au/story/7645072/pm-takes-joint-control-of-nsw-liberals-can-choose-candidates/?cs=14264 |archive-date=28 March 2022}}{{cite web |last=Cockburn |first=Gerard |date=27 March 2022 |title=Scott Morrison, Dominic Perrottet and Christine McDiven take over NSW Liberals branch for second time in a month |url=https://www.canberratimes.com.au/story/7674988/federal-liberals-take-over-nsw-branch-again/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220328081857/https://www.canberratimes.com.au/story/7674988/federal-liberals-take-over-nsw-branch-again/ |archive-date=28 March 2022 |access-date=29 March 2022 |newspaper=The Canberra Times |url-access=subscription}} While the Liberal state executive was dissolved, the committee was allowed to "hand-pick" party candidates for the election and bypass local pre-selection ballots. On the same day as the replacements for Kitching and Carr were finalised, the National Executive "[[Parachute candidate|parachuted]]" [[Andrew Charlton (politician)|Andrew Charlton]] into the [[Division of Parramatta]] in New South Wales, bypassing a local preselection with three candidates from diverse ethnic backgrounds. This prompted a backlash from local party members and the incumbent retiring Labor member for Parramatta [[Julie Owens]].{{cite news |last=McGowan |first=Michael |date=29 March 2022 |title=Disillusionment grows within Labor about the party's commitment to cultural diversity |newspaper=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2022/mar/29/disillusionment-grows-within-labor-about-the-partys-commitment-to-cultural-diversity |url-status=live |access-date=30 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220330004515/https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2022/mar/29/disillusionment-grows-within-labor-about-the-partys-commitment-to-cultural-diversity |archive-date=30 March 2022}} ===Independents=== {{Main|Independent politicians in Australia}} In the [[2013 Australian federal election|2013 federal election]], the [[Voices for Indi]] organisation successfully backed independent candidate [[Cathy McGowan (politician)|Cathy McGowan]] to defeat the incumbent Liberal member of parliament [[Sophie Mirabella]] in the [[Division of Indi]]. McGowan was reelected in 2016, retiring after two terms to be succeeded by fellow independent [[Helen Haines]]. McGowan's victory inspired the campaign of independent [[Zali Steggall]] in [[2019 Australian federal election|2019]], who defeated the Liberal former Prime Minister [[Tony Abbott]] in the seat of [[Division of Warringah|Warringah]]. In addition to Haines and Steggall's campaigns for reelection, the 2022 election saw the candidacy of several challengers who were in turn inspired by Steggall.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/05/19/world/australia/federal-election-independents.html|title=How a Group of Female Independents Aims to Revive Australian Democracy|work=The New York Times|date=19 May 2022 |access-date=22 May 2022|last1=Cave |first1=Damien }} Termed "[[teal independents]]" (denoting a mix of [[classical liberal]] blue and [[environmentalist]] green), these candidates contested in Liberal heartlands notably including [[Division of Curtin|Curtin]], [[Division of Goldstein|Goldstein]], [[Division of Kooyong|Kooyong]], [[Division of Mackellar|Mackellar]], [[Division of North Sydney|North Sydney]] and [[Division of Wentworth|Wentworth]]. Each received funds from the political fundraising group [[Climate 200]].{{cite news |last1=Millar |first1=Royce |title=A secret party? Immoral? Explaining who the 'teal' independents really are |url=https://www.smh.com.au/politics/federal/a-secret-party-immoral-explaining-who-the-teal-independents-really-are-20220505-p5aio4.html |access-date=6 May 2022 |work=The Sydney Morning Herald |date=6 May 2022}} ==Electoral system== Members of the House of Representatives are elected by [[instant-runoff voting]], which in Australia is known as full preferential voting. Each [[Divisions of the Australian House of Representatives|electorate]] elects one member. Senators are elected by [[single transferable vote]] and [[proportional representation]]. In states senators are elected from state-wide six-member districts, and in territories from territory-wide two-member districts. Ballots are counted at least twice, at the polling place and, starting Monday night after election day, at counting centres.{{Cite web |title=House of Representatives count |url=https://aec.gov.au/Voting/counting/hor.htm |access-date=2022-08-27 |website=Australian Electoral Commission |language=en-AU}}{{Cite web |title=The Senate counting process |url=https://aec.gov.au/Voting/counting/senate.htm |access-date=2022-08-27 |website=Australian Electoral Commission |language=en-AU}} == State of electorates == ===Redistribution=== {{see also|Divisions of the Australian House of Representatives|Redistribution (Australia)}} [[File:Australian electoral divisions, blank map (2022).svg|thumb|Map of the 151 electoral divisions to the House of Representatives (blank) in use for the 2022 federal election]] The [[Australian Electoral Commission]] is required, one year after the first sitting day for a new House of Representatives, to determine the number of members to which each State and Territory is entitled. If the number in any state changes, a redistribution will be required in those states. A redistribution will be postponed if it would begin within one year of the expiration of the House of Representatives. Demographic statistics for December 2019 released by the [[Australian Bureau of Statistics]] on 18 June 2020 were used to calculate the determination. The population counts confirmed that the number of seats in the House of Representatives was to return to 150, with Victoria gaining a seat (39), and Western Australia (15) and the Northern Territory (1) losing a seat each.{{cite web|last = Green|first = Antony|author-link = Antony Green|title = ABS Population Statistics Confirm Changes in House Representation|url = ==Voter registration== Enrollment of eligible voters is compulsory. Voters must notify the AEC within 8 weeks of a change of address or after turning 18. The electoral rolls are closed for new enrollments or update of details about a week after the issue of [[Writ of election#Australia|writs for election]].{{cite web|url = http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/cea1918233/s155.html|work = [[Commonwealth Electoral Act 1918]]|title = Section 155: Date for close of Rolls|publisher = [[Australasian Legal Information Institute]] (AustLII)|access-date = 2 April 2021|archive-date = 31 July 2017|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20170731082910/http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/cea1918233/s155.html|url-status = live}} Enrollment is optional for 16- or 17-year-olds, but they cannot vote until they turn 18,{{cite web|url=https://www.aec.gov.au/enrol/|title=Enrol to vote|website=Australian Electoral Commission|access-date=23 April 2021|archive-date=1 October 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191001230634/https://www.aec.gov.au/enrol/|url-status=live}} and persons who have applied for Australian citizenship may also apply for provisional enrollment which takes effect on the granting of citizenship.{{Cite Legislation AU |Cth|act|cea1918233|Commonwealth Electoral Act 1918|99a}} A total of 17,228,900 people were enrolled to vote in the election, which meant that 96.8% of all eligible Australians were enrolled on the electoral roll.{{cite web|url=https://www.aec.gov.au/media/2022/04-21.htm|title=Final enrolment numbers now available|work=aec.gov.au|date=21 April 2022|access-date=21 April 2022|archive-date=21 April The winner of the debate was to be decided through a viewer poll hosted on Channel 9's website. Although 49% of viewers preferred Albanese to be the better prime minister compared to 45% preferring Morrison, the debate was a 50–50 draw.{{cite web|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-05-08/scott-morrison-anthony-albanese-second-leaders-debate/101048046#live-blog-post-1211130143|title=Federal election: Scott Morrison and Anthony Albanese face off in second leaders' debate — as it happened|work=ABC News|first1=Jessica|last1=Riga|first2=Georgia|last2=Hitch|date=8 May 2022|access-date=8 May 2022}} Channel 9's moderation of the debate was subject to widespread criticism, with both Morrison and Albanese shouting over the top of one another and the moderator, and for the technical issues experienced by a web page run by Channel 9 to gather audience opinion.
