== Aftermath ==
[[File:Valkö på valdagen 2022.jpg|thumb|alt=Hundreds queue to vote at Stockholm Central Station, 35 minutes before closing time, on election day, 11 September 2022|Hundreds queue to vote at [[Stockholm Central Station]], 35 minutes before closing time, on election day, 11 September 2022]]
Voting stations were opened from 08:00 ([[Central European Summer Time|CEST]]) to 20:00, and there were 7,772,120 [[Swedish nationals]] in total that had the right to vote in the 2022 general election.<ref>{{cite web|date=11 September 2022|title=Sweden heads to polls as ruling Social Democrats face challenge from far right|url=https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20220911-swedes-head-to-polls-in-tight-election-race-marked-by-crime-and-the-energy-crisis|access-date=11 September 2022|website=France 24|archive-date=11 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911094522/https://www.france24.com/en/europe/20220911-swedes-head-to-polls-in-tight-election-race-marked-by-crime-and-the-energy-crisis|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Rådata och statistik|url=https://val.se/valresultat/riksdag-region-och-kommun/2022/radata-och-statistik.html|access-date=11 September 2022|website=Valmyndigheten|language=sv|archive-date=11 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911094523/https://www.val.se/valresultat/riksdag-region-och-kommun/2022/radata-och-statistik.html|url-status=live}}</ref> According to [[exit polls]] that were published by [[Sveriges Television]] and [[TV4 (Swedish TV channel)|TV4]], the bloc around the [[Swedish Social Democratic Party]] (S) showed a tight lead against the bloc around the [[Moderate Party]] (M).<ref>{{cite news|last=Milne|first=Richard|date=11 September 2022|title=Swedish election result too close to call|work=Financial Times|url=https://www.ft.com/content/c752cdfa-7fd1-4413-a3a7-bfb459a430a0|access-date=11 September 2022|archive-date=11 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911204719/https://www.ft.com/content/c752cdfa-7fd1-4413-a3a7-bfb459a430a0|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|date=11 September 2022|title=Sweden's centre-left bloc leading election, TV4 poll shows|publisher=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/swedens-centre-left-bloc-leading-election-tv4-poll-2022-09-11/|access-date=11 September 2022|archive-date=11 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911204840/https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/swedens-centre-left-bloc-leading-election-tv4-poll-2022-09-11/|url-status=live}}</ref> It was also reported that the [[Sweden Democrats]] (SD) surpassed M in the number of votes, and suggested that it could become the second-largest parliamentary party.<ref>{{cite web|last=Crouch|first=David|date=11 September 2022|title=Rightwing bloc heading to victory in Swedish election, 90% of vote count suggests|url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/sep/11/swedish-election-exit-polls-far-right|access-date=11 September 2022|website=The Guardian|archive-date=11 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911204719/https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/sep/11/swedish-election-exit-polls-far-right|url-status=live}}</ref> S also won more votes in comparison with the [[2018 Swedish general election]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Binley|first1=Alex|last2=Maishman|first2=Elsa|date=12 September 2022|title=Sweden election: Result could take days as vote too close to call|publisher=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-62872545|access-date=12 September 2022|archive-date=12 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220912093649/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-62872545|url-status=live}}</ref>

Sweden's [[Election Authority (Sweden)|Election Authority]] stated that the bloc that composed of M, SD, [[Christian Democrats (Sweden)|Christian Democrats]] (KD), and [[Liberals (Sweden)|Liberals]] (L) overtook the bloc around S by one to three seats during the counting of the preliminary results.<ref>{{cite web|last=Jungstedt|first=Christopher|date=11 September 2022|title=Sweden Opposition Overtakes Premier's Bloc in Early Vote Tally|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-09-11/sweden-opposition-overtakes-premier-s-bloc-in-early-vote-tally|access-date=11 September 2022|website=Bloomberg}}</ref> The gap between the two blocs was around 50,000 votes.<ref>{{cite web|last=Duxbury|first=Charlie|date=11 September 2022|title=Sweden's right-wing opposition bloc leads tight election|url=https://www.politico.eu/article/swedens-ruling-center-left-takes-slim-lead-in-national-vote-exit-poll/|access-date=11 September 2022|website=Politico|archive-date=11 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911234729/https://www.politico.eu/article/swedens-ruling-center-left-takes-slim-lead-in-national-vote-exit-poll/|url-status=live}}</ref> [[Ulf Kristersson]], the M leader, stated that "the results would be likely known by Wednesday" and he thanked his voters, while [[Jimmie Åkesson]], the SD leader, stated that SD would play a "central role" in the power shift.<ref>{{cite news|date=11 September 2022|title=Swedish Moderates leader says election result won't come until Wednesday|publisher=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/swedish-moderates-leader-says-election-result-wont-come-until-wednesday-2022-09-11/|access-date=11 September 2022|archive-date=11 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911233519/https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/swedish-moderates-leader-says-election-result-wont-come-until-wednesday-2022-09-11/|url-status=live}}</ref> Kristersson also said that a change in the numbers of seats is possible.<ref>{{cite web|date=3 June 2022|title=Senaste nytt om svensk politik och valet 2022|url=https://www.dn.se/sverige/senaste-nytt-om-valet-2022/|access-date=11 September 2022|website=Dagens Nyheter|language=sv|archive-date=11 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911235030/https://www.dn.se/sverige/senaste-nytt-om-valet-2022/|url-status=live}}</ref> As overseas and some postal votes were to be counted, the incumbent prime minister [[Magdalena Andersson]] stated that "it is too close to call the election".<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ahlander |first1=Johan |last2=Johnson |first2=Simon |last3=Pollard |first3=Niklas |title=Swedish right opposition inches ahead in election cliff-hanger |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/swedes-head-polls-close-run-election-marked-by-crime-energy-crisis-2022-09-10/ |url-status=live |publisher=Reuters |date=11 September 2022 |access-date=12 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220911094521/https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/swedes-head-polls-close-run-election-marked-by-crime-energy-crisis-2022-09-10/ |archive-date=11 September 2022}}</ref> Some analysts have seen the rise of the [[Nuance Party]], mainly aimed at the country's Muslim population, as one of the causes of the losses in the left bloc.<ref>{{cite web|last=Kenez|first=Levent|date=14 September 2022|url=https://nordicmonitor.com/2022/09/pro-erdogan-islamist-party-in-sweden-raises-concern-as-highly-voted-in-immigrant-districts/|title=Pro-Erdoğan Islamist party in Sweden sparks concerns after it receives large number of votes in immigrant districts|website=Nordic Monitor|access-date=17 September 2022|archive-date=13 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220913220734/https://nordicmonitor.com/2022/09/pro-erdogan-islamist-party-in-sweden-raises-concern-as-highly-voted-in-immigrant-districts/|url-status=live}}</ref>

SD's election night vigil in Stockholm attracted controversy after the party refused to grant access to several foreign language media and after the party's chief of staff [[Linus Bylund]] joked that he was looking forward to "journalist rugby", where "you push journalists around".<ref>{{cite web|date=15 September 2022|title=Sweden: RSF asks the country's second biggest party to stop undermining press freedom and right to information|url=https://rsf.org/en/sweden-rsf-asks-country-s-second-biggest-party-stop-undermining-press-freedom-and-right-information|access-date=25 October 2022|work=Reporters Without Borders}}</ref> The election vigil also attracted controversy after SD politician [[Rebecka Fallenkvist]] proclaimed {{lang|sv|"Helg Seger"}} while raising her arm in an interview with far-right blog ''[[Samnytt]]'', which is phonetically similar to {{lang|sv|"Hell Seger"}}, the Swedish translation of the Nazi "[[Sieg Heil]]" chant. Fallenkvist subsequently told {{lang|sv|[[Expressen]]}} that she had aimed to provoke the media into overinterpretations before later telling {{lang|sv|[[Dagens Nyheter]]}} that she had misspoke and meant to say {{lang|sv|"segerhelg"}}, which would translate to "victory weekend".<ref>{{cite web|date=13 September 2022|title=Sweden Democrat politician accused of Nazi slogan in election night clip|url=https://www.thelocal.se/20220913/sd-mini-scandals-helg-seger-journalist-rugby-and-akesson-for-pm/|access-date=13 September 2022|work=The Local Sweden|archive-date=13 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220913092649/https://www.thelocal.se/20220913/sd-mini-scandals-helg-seger-journalist-rugby-and-akesson-for-pm/|url-status=live}}</ref> In late October, an SD candidate who had been elected to the [[Nynäshamn]] City Council resigned as a councillor after a media investigation found that she had been an active member of the neo-Nazi [[Nordic Resistance Movement]] for two decades.<ref>{{cite web|date=28 October 2022|title=Sweden Democrat councillor resigns after outing as neo-Nazi propagandist|url=https://www.thelocal.se/20221028/sweden-democrat-councillor-outed-as-active-neo-nazi-propagandist/|access-date=13 September 2022|work=The Local Sweden}}</ref>

On 13 September [[Annie Lööf]], the leader of the [[Centre Party (Sweden)|Centre Party]] (C), sent an internal email to the party's elected politicians in which she called the results for the party "very disappointing" and stated that C's board would conduct an investigation into the party's campaign.<ref>{{cite news|last=Schau|first=Oscar|date=13 September 2022|title=Annie Lööf i internt mejl till partiet: 'Självrannsakan'|url=https://www.svt.se/nyheter/inrikes/annie-loof-i-internt-krismejl-sjalvrannsakan|access-date=13 September 2022|work=SVT Nyheter|archive-date=13 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220913185815/https://www.svt.se/nyheter/inrikes/annie-loof-i-internt-krismejl-sjalvrannsakan|url-status=live}}</ref> Two days later, Lööf announced her resignation as party leader.<ref>{{cite web|date=15 September 2022|title=Annie Lööf avgår som partiledare|url=https://www.aftonbladet.se/a/69zo3r|access-date=15 September 2022|website=Aftonbladet|language=sv|archive-date=19 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220919130235/https://www.aftonbladet.se/nyheter/a/69zo3r/annie-loof-kallar-till-prestraff|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|date=15 September 2022|title=Lööf avgår som C-ledare|language=sv|work=SVT Nyheter|url=https://www.svt.se/nyheter/snabbkollen/loof-avgar-som-c-ledare|access-date=15 September 2022|archive-date=15 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220915115858/https://www.svt.se/nyheter/snabbkollen/loof-avgar-som-c-ledare|url-status=live}}</ref> Andersson conceded on 14 September,<ref>{{cite web|date=14 September 2022|title=Sweden election: PM Magdalena Andersson concedes victory to right-wing opposition|url=https://www.dw.com/en/sweden-election-pm-magdalena-andersson-concedes-victory-to-right-wing-opposition/a-63117673|access-date=14 September 2022|website=Deutsche Welle|archive-date=14 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220914183505/https://www.dw.com/en/sweden-election-pm-magdalena-andersson-concedes-victory-to-right-wing-opposition/a-63117673|url-status=live}}</ref> and announced her resignation as prime minister,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.expressen.se/nyheter/val-2022/efter-valforlusten-andersson-avgar-/|title=Efter valförlusten: Andersson avgår|trans-title=After the election loss: Andersson resigns|last=Holm|first=Gusten|website=Expressen|language=sv|date=14 September 2022|access-date=17 September 2022|archive-date=15 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220915195232/https://www.expressen.se/nyheter/val-2022/efter-valforlusten-andersson-avgar-/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=14 September 2022|title=Swedish PM resigns as right-wing parties win vote|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-62908902|access-date=14 September 2022|publisher=BBC News|archive-date=14 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220914204453/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-62908902|url-status=live}}</ref> paving the way for Kristersson to attempt to form a new government. Andersson called upon M, KD, and L to reject SD, and said she was open to a government with M that would exclude SD.<ref>{{cite web |last=Larsson |first=Astrid |title=Magdalena Andersson avgår: Dörr öppen för Kristersson |trans-title=Magdalena Andersson resigns: Door open for Kristersson |url=https://www.expressen.se/nyheter/magdalena-andersson-avgar--dorr-oppen-for-kristersson/ |url-status=live |website=Expressen |date=15 September 2022|access-date=17 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220915104055/https://www.expressen.se/nyheter/magdalena-andersson-avgar--dorr-oppen-for-kristersson/ |archive-date=15 September 2022 |language=sv}}</ref> Some Liberals in particular have been wary of a government with SD.<ref>{{cite web |last=<nowiki>Reuters</nowiki>kiöld |first=Annie |title=Pourmokhtari (L) lovar att fälla regering där SD ingår |url=https://www.dn.se/sverige/pourmokhtari-l-lovar-att-falla-regering-dar-sd-ingar/ |url-status=live |website=Dagens Nyheter |date=14 September 2022 |access-date=17 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220915191802/https://www.dn.se/sverige/pourmokhtari-l-lovar-att-falla-regering-dar-sd-ingar/ |archive-date=15 September 2022 |language=sv}}</ref> [[Renew Europe]], the [[European parliamentary group]] of which L is part, has been critical of the Liberals being part of a government including SD.<ref>{{cite web |last1=<nowiki>Reuters</nowiki>kiöld |first1=Annie |last2=Gripenberg |first2=Pia |last3=Melchior |first3=Sigrid |title=Johan Pehrson vädjar till EU-kollegor efter kritik om SD-samröre |url=https://www.dn.se/sverige/johan-pehrson-vadjar-till-eu-kollegor-efter-sd-kritik/ |url-status=live |website=Dagens Nyheter |date=17 September 2022 |access-date=17 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220917171619/https://www.dn.se/sverige/johan-pehrson-vadjar-till-eu-kollegor-efter-sd-kritik/ |archive-date=17 September 2022 |language=sv}}</ref>

Despite the right-wing majority, no government had been formed by the opening of the newly elected [[Riksdag]] on 26 September. Moderate Party leaders raised concerns that SD would hold a disproportionate amount of influence over a new government, and would use the committee chairmanships allocated to them to block or delay government policy.<ref>{{cite web|date=26 September 2022|title=Källor: M oroliga att SD får för mycket makt: 'Kommer bli extremt stökigt'|url=https://omni.se/kallor-m-oroliga-att-sd-far-for-mycket-makt-kommer-bli-extremt-stokigt/a/15725M|url-status=live|access-date=26 September 2022|website=Omni|language=sv|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220926222403/https://omni.se/kallor-m-oroliga-att-sd-far-for-mycket-makt-kommer-bli-extremt-stokigt/a/15725M|archive-date=26 September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=26 September 2022|title=M-källor: Kan bli stökigt när SD intar utskotten|url=https://www.aftonbladet.se/a/0Q41no|access-date=26 September 2022|website=Aftonbladet|language=sv|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220926222422/https://www.aftonbladet.se/nyheter/a/0Q41no/m-kallor-kan-bli-stokigt-nar-sd-intar-utskotten|archive-date=26 September 2022}}</ref> On 26 September [[Andreas Norlén]] of the Moderate Party was re-elected as [[Speaker of the Riksdag]] by acclamation. The election of [[Julia Kronlid]] of the Sweden Democrats as [[Second Deputy Speaker of the Riksdag]] required a second ballot after the first ballot fell three votes short of the required majority.<ref>{{cite web|date=26 September 2022|title=Andreas Norlén omvald – SD får talmanspost|url=https://www.fokus.se/politik/andreas-norlen-omvald-sd-far-talmanspost/|url-status=live|access-date=27 September 2022|website=Fokus|language=sv|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220927004119/https://www.fokus.se/politik/andreas-norlen-omvald-sd-far-talmanspost/|archive-date=27 September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|date=26 September 2022|title=Andreas Norlén omvald till talman|language=sv|publisher=Sveriges Radio|url=https://sverigesradio.se/artikel/andreas-norlen-omvald-till-talman|url-status=live|access-date=27 September 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220927004229/https://sverigesradio.se/artikel/andreas-norlen-omvald-till-talman|archive-date=27 September 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=26 September 2022|title=Andreas Norlén (M) omvald till talman – möttes av applåder|url=https://www.aftonbladet.se/a/nQwEwm|url-status=live|access-date=27 September 2022|website=Aftonbladet|language=sv|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220926111644/https://www.aftonbladet.se/nyheter/a/nQwEwm/andreas-norlen-vald-till-talman|archive-date=26 September 2022}}</ref>

=== Government formation ===
[[File:Ulf Kristersson in october 2022 (5 av 7).jpg|thumb|218x218px|Kristersson on his way to the Speaker, October 2022]]
On 19 September, Speaker [[Andreas Norlén]], after talks with representatives of the Riksdag parties and a discussion with the Deputy Speakers, tasked [[Ulf Kristersson]] of the [[Moderate Party]] (M) with probing the conditions for forming a government.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Riksdagsförvaltningen |title=Pressmeddelande: Talmannen ger sonderingsuppdrag till Ulf Kristersson |url=https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/press/pressmeddelanden/2022/sep/19/pressmeddelande-talmannen-ger-sonderingsuppdrag-till-ulf-kristersson/ |access-date=13 October 2022 |website=Riksdagen |language=sv}}</ref> On 12 October, Kristersson reported to the speaker and requested two more days to get his government documents together.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ulf Kristersson efter mötet med talmannen: Behöver två dagar till |url=https://www.aftonbladet.se/a/MoLzMr |access-date=13 October 2022 |website=www.aftonbladet.se |date=12 October 2022 |language=sv}}</ref> On 14 October, Kristersson announced to the Speaker of the Riksdag that he was ready to form a government with the [[Christian Democrats (Sweden)|Christian Democrats]] (KD) and the [[Liberals (Sweden)|Liberals]] (L), with the support of the [[Sweden Democrats]] (SD). The four parties' written agreement with Kristersson as Prime Minister for the 2022–2026 term is called the [[Tidö Agreement]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Persson |first=Ida |date=14 October 2022 |title=L, KD och M ska ingå i regeringen – SD får stort inflytande |trans-title=L, KD and M will be included in the government – SD gets large influence |language=sv |work=[[SVT Nyheter]] |url=https://www.svt.se/nyheter/inrikes/l-kd-och-m-ska-inga-i-regeringen-sd-far-stort-inflytande |access-date=14 October 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=14 October 2022 |title=Så blir Tidöavtalet: Liberalerna i regeringen – SD utanför |trans-title=What the Tidö Agreement will be: The Liberals in the government – SD excluded |url=https://www.dn.se/sverige/tidoavtalet-liberalerna-i-regeringen-sd-utanfor/ |url-access=subscription |access-date=14 October 2022 |website=[[Dagens Nyheter]] |language=sv}}</ref> With the agreement, named after the place where it was negotiated, this is the first time SD have formalised influence over a government's policy.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.cision.com/se/liberalerna/r/overenskommelse-for-sverige---tidoavtalet,c3648119|url-status=live|title=Överenskommelse för Sverige – Tidöavtalet|trans-title=Agreement for Sweden – the Tidö Agreement|website=Cision News|language=sv|date=14 October 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221018052038/https://news.cision.com/se/liberalerna/r/overenskommelse-for-sverige---tidoavtalet,c3648119|archive-date=18 October 2022|access-date=18 October 2022}}</ref>

On 17 October, the Riksdag voted 176 to 173 in favour of Kristersson becoming prime minister under the four parties' agreement.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://apnews.com/article/elections-sweden-government-and-politics-945104209e78dd5722aacbfe9eebbf2c|title=Sweden's parliament elects conservative prime minister|url-status=live|website=[[AP News]]|publisher=[[Associated Press]]|date=17 October 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221017143254/https://apnews.com/article/elections-sweden-government-and-politics-945104209e78dd5722aacbfe9eebbf2c|archive-date=17 October 2022|access-date=19 October 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.dw.com/en/sweden-lawmakers-elect-ulf-kristersson-as-prime-minister/a-63461080|url-status=live|title=Swedish parliament elects conservative PM|publisher=[[Deutsche Welle]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221017142623/https://www.dw.com/en/sweden-lawmakers-elect-ulf-kristersson-as-prime-minister/a-63461080|archive-date=17 October 2022|access-date=19 October 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Cursino|first=Malu|date=17 October 2022|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-63289903|url-status=live|title=Ulf Kristersson: Swedish parliament elects new PM backed by far right|publisher=BBC News|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221017154017/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-63289903|archive-date=17 October 2022|access-date=19 October 2022}}</ref> As a government, M, KD, and L together have fewer seats than the [[Swedish Social Democratic Party]] (S) and must rely on SD for every vote. Parliament of Turkey|elected members]] | outgoing_members = [[27th Parliament of Turkey|outgoing members]] }} Parliamentary elections were held in Turkey on 14 May 2023, alongside [[2023 Turkish presidential election|presidential elections]], to elect all 600 members of the [[Grand National Assembly of Turkey|Grand National Assembly]]. The incoming members formed the [[28th Parliament of Turkey]]. The elections had originally been scheduled to take place on June 18, but the government moved them forward by a month to avoid coinciding with the university exams, the [[Hajj|Hajj pilgrimage]] and the start of the [[summer vacation|summer holidays]].{{cite news |title=Erdogan calls Turkish elections for May 14, three months after quake disaster |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/erdogan-officially-calls-turkish-elections-may-14-2023-03-10/ |access-date=19 May 2023 |work=Reuters |date=10 March 2023 |language=en}} Prior to the election, the [[electoral threshold]] for a party to enter parliament was lowered from 10% to 7% by the ruling party.{{cite news |title=Turkey reduces election threshold to 7 percent - Türkiye News |url=https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/turkish-parliament-approves-election-law-changes-172648 |access-date=19 May 2023 |work=Hürriyet Daily News |date=1 April 2022 |language=en}} The elections were contested by a total of 24 political parties. Some parties decided to participate in the elections as part of an [[electoral alliance]], many of which were formed for the previous [[2018 Turkish parliamentary election|2018 election]] and had been expanded since. The governing [[Justice and Development Party (Turkey)|Justice and Development Party]] (AKP) of incumbent President [[Recep Tayyip Erdoğan]] lead the [[People's Alliance (Turkey)|People's Alliance]], which also included the [[Nationalist Movement Party]] (MHP), the [[Great Union Party]] (BBP) and the [[New Welfare Party]] (YRP). The largest opposition alliance was headed by the main opposition [[Republican People's Party]] (CHP) and included five other parties. These included the [[Good Party]] (İYİ), the [[Felicity Party]] (SP), the [[Democrat Party (Turkey, current)|Democrat Party]] (DP) and two other parties headed by former senior AKP politicians, namely the [[Democracy and Progress Party]] (DEVA) of former economy minister [[Ali Babacan]] and the [[Future Party (Turkey)|Future Party]] (GP) of former Prime Minister [[Ahmet Davutoğlu]].{{cn|date=May 2023}} The pro-Kurdish [[Peoples' Democratic Party (Turkey)|Peoples' Democratic Party]] (HDP) opted to run on the lists of the [[Party of Greens and the Left Future]] (YSGP) in light of a potential closure case. The YSGP itself headed the left-wing [[Labour and Freedom Alliance]] along with the [[Workers' Party of Turkey (2017)|Workers' Party of Turkey]] (TİP). Two smaller alliances, the [[Ancestral Alliance]] of presidential candidate [[Sinan Oğan]] and the [[Union of Socialist Forces]], also participated in the elections for the first time.{{cite news |last1=Gadzhiev |first1=Amur |title=Turkey on the Eve of Presidential and Parliamentary Elections: Balance of Political Forces in the Country |url=https://russiancouncil.ru/en/analytics-and-comments/analytics/turkey-on-the-eve-of-presidential-and-parliamentary-elections-balance-of-political-forces-in-the-cou/?sphrase_id=97812031 |access-date=19 May 2023 |work=russiancouncil.ru |date=19 April 2023 |language=en}} The People's Alliance retained its majority in the parliament with 323 MPs. The AKP, led by incumbent president Erdoğan, won the highest percentage of the vote with 36%, though it suffered its worst result since 2002. MHP, the second largest party of the People's Alliance, outperformed expectations and won 10.1% of the votes. The alliance overall won just under 50% of the vote. The Nation Alliance only marginally improved on its 2018 vote, winning a combined 34% and 212 MPs. The Labour and Freedom Alliance suffered a decline in their vote, winning just over 10% and 66 seats. No other electoral alliance won seats. The election resulted in seven parties entering the parliament, which is a record in Turkish politics.{{cn|date=May 2023}} Many smaller parties ran on the lists of larger ones to avoid splitting the vote. Prior to the election, the CHP caused controversy by fielding 77 DEVA, Felicity Party, Future Party, and Democrat Party candidates on its own lists, of which 39 (14 DEVA, 10 Felicity, 10 Future, 3 Democrats, 1 [[Good Party|IYI]], and 1 [[Party for Change in Turkey]]) were elected — a significantly higher proportion than these parties' national share of support.{{Cite web |title=Millet İttifakı partilerinden 39 aday, CHP listesinden Meclis'e girdi |url=https://www.ntv.com.tr/2023-secim/millet-ittifaki-partilerinden-39-aday-chp-listesinden-meclise-girdi,JbVkFy3fXU2HhSMmTjmwLQ |access-date=2023-10-07 |website=www.ntv.com.tr |language=tr}} These included former AKP ministers such as [[Sadullah Ergin]] (running as a DEVA candidate), who was widely criticised for his role as Justice Minister in the [[Ergenekon (allegation)|Ergenekon]] conspiracy against the [[Turkish Armed Forces]]. The AKP, meanwhile, was criticised for fielding members of the [[Free Cause Party]] (HÜDA PAR), a party known for its ties to the [[Kurdish Hezbollah]], as candidates.{{cn|date=May 2023}} ==Electoral system== The 600 members of the [[Grand National Assembly of Turkey]] will be elected by [[party-list proportional representation]] in [[Electoral districts of Turkey|87 electoral districts]], by the [[D'Hondt method]]. For the purpose of legislative elections, 77 of Turkey's 81 provinces serve as single districts. Due to their large populations, the provinces of [[Bursa]] and [[İzmir]] are divided into two districts, while the provinces of [[Ankara]] and [[Istanbul]] are each divided into three.{{cite web |title=How Turkey's Parliamentary Elections Work |url=https://carnegieeurope.eu/2015/10/26/how-turkey-s-parliamentary-elections-work-pub-61744 |website=carnegieeurope.eu |access-date=19 May 2023 |date=26 October 2015}} According to the [[Constitution of Turkey]], any amendment to the election law can only apply a year after it comes into effect.{{cite web |title=Turkey: Parliament Passes Law Amending Election Laws and Lowering Electoral Threshold |url=https://www.loc.gov/item/global-legal-monitor/2022-04-24/turkey-parliament-passes-law-amending-election-laws-and-lowering-electoral-threshold/#:~:text=Significantly%2C%20because%20article%2067%2F7,affect%20the%20upcoming%20general%20elections. |website=Library of Congress, Washington, D.C. 20540 USA |access-date=19 May 2023}} ===Lowering of the electoral threshold=== At the initiative of the ruling [[Justice and Development Party (Turkey)|AKP]] and its main political ally [[Nationalist Movement Party|MHP]], the national [[electoral threshold]] for a party to enter parliament was lowered from 10% to 7%.{{cite web |title=Turkey reduces its election threshold from 10 to 7 percent |work=Turkish Minute |date=April 2022 |url=https://www.turkishminute.com/2022/04/01/key-reduces-its-election-threshold-from-10-to-7-percent/ |access-date=2 April 2022}} This was the first lowering of the threshold since it was introduced by the military junta following the [[1980 Turkish coup d'état]].{{cite news |title=Turkey lowers party' election threshold for parliament to 7 pct |url=http://www.xinhuanet.com/english/europe/20220401/bc9feecf552b4d299c872212b9a91614/c.html |access-date=2 April 2022 |work=www.xinhuanet.com |date=1 April 2022}} There is no threshold for [[Independent (politician)|independent]] candidates.{{Cite web|url=https://www.electoral-reform.org.uk/crossing-the-threshold-the-turkish-election/|title=Crossing the threshold – the Turkish election|website=www.electoral-reform.org.uk|language=en-US|access-date=3 March 2020}} Political parties can also opt to contest the election in a [[political alliance]] with other parties, removing the 7% requirement as long as the alliance as a whole wins more than 7% of the vote in total.{{cite news |title=Yeni seçim yasası ve ittifaklar: Kritik değişiklikler! |url=https://www.ntv.com.tr/galeri/2023-secim/yeni-secim-yasasi-ve-ittifaklar-kritik-degisiklikler,nqnTTxMu8E6LG1P7HUnh6w |access-date=19 May 2023 |work=www.ntv.com.tr |date=3 April 2023 |language=tr}} Other amendments to the election law includes the distribution of seats. Previously, parliamentary seats were distributed based on the vote share of each election alliance in any given district. Now, the seats are distributed based solely on the vote share of each political party in that district. If applied to the previous elections, the results would have been slightly more in line with the preferences of the voters on local level. For example, one [[Erzurum (electoral district)|Erzurum seat]] from [[Good Party|IYI]] (4th largest party in Erzurum) would have gone to [[Peoples' Democratic Party (Turkey)|HDP]] (3rd largest party in Erzurum) and one [[Elazığ (electoral district)|Elazığ seat]] from [[Republican People's Party|CHP]] (3rd largest party in Elazığ) to [[Nationalist Movement Party|MHP]] (2nd largest party in Elazığ).{{cite news |last1=Sarıkaya |first1=Muharrem |title=İttifakın ayrıcalığı kalmayacak |url=https://www.haberturk.com/yazarlar/muharrem-sarikaya/3375130-ittifakin-ayricaligi-kalmayacak |access-date=2 April 2022 |work=www.haberturk.com |date=15 March 2022 |language=tr}} ===Electoral districts=== {{Main|Electoral districts of Turkey}} Turkey is split into 87 [[electoral district]]s, which elect a certain number of [[Members of Parliament#Turkey|members]] to the [[Grand National Assembly of Turkey]]. The Assembly has a total of 600 seats, with each electoral district allocated a certain number of MPs in proportion to their population. The [[Supreme Electoral Council of Turkey]] conducts population reviews of each district before the election and can increase or decrease a district's number of seats according to their electorate. In all but four cases, electoral districts share the same name and borders as the 81 [[Provinces of Turkey|provinces]], with the exceptions being [[Ankara]], [[Bursa]], [[İzmir]] and [[Istanbul]]. Provinces electing between 19 and 36 MPs are split into two electoral districts, while any province electing above 36 MPs is divided into three. As the country's most populous provinces, Bursa and İzmir are divided into two subdistricts while Ankara and Istanbul are divided into three. violence === During the election campaign, several occurrences that took place have been labelled as political violence. On 31 March 2023, the [[Istanbul]] headquarters of the Good Party was targeted in a shooting attack.{{Cite web |date=31 March 2023 |title=Son Dakika: İYİ Parti İstanbul İl Başkanlığı'na silahlı saldırı |url=https://www.cumhuriyet.com.tr/turkiye/son-dakika-iyi-parti-istanbul-il-baskanligina-silahli-saldiri-2066680 |access-date=31 March 2023 |website=www.cumhuriyet.com.tr |language=tr |archive-date=31 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230331145610/https://www.cumhuriyet.com.tr/turkiye/son-dakika-iyi-parti-istanbul-il-baskanligina-silahli-saldiri-2066680 |url-status=live }} No one was harmed in the shooting. Akşener criticised Erdoğan after the attack by saying "A political party cannot be intimidated one and a half months before an election. We are not afraid. I fear nothing but God. Mr. Recep (Erdoğan), I am not afraid of you. But you are the president and you are responsible for every citizen in this country." The attackers were emboldened by the president's harsh words against the opposition, Akşener said.{{Cite web |date=31 March 2023 |title="I am not afraid, Mr. Recep!" |url=https://www.gerceknews.com/turkey/i-am-not-afraid-mr-recep-219422h |access-date=31 March 2023 |website=Gercek News |language=en |archive-date=31 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230331145623/https://www.gerceknews.com/turkey/i-am-not-afraid-mr-recep-219422h |url-status=live }}{{Cite web |date=31 March 2023 |title=Son Dakika: Meral Akşener İl Başkanlığı'nda... President Erdoğan said in response to Akşener "The truth has come out, are you now going to apologize to me?"{{cite news |title=Cumhurbaşkanı Erdoğan'dan Akşener'e kurşun tepkisi: Gerçek ortaya çıktı, özür dileyecek misin? |url=https://www.ntv.com.tr/turkiye/cumhurbaskani-erdogandan-aksenere-kursun-tepkisi-gercek-ortaya-cikti-ozur-dileyecek-misin,ak7MbXYnrUy6J4V0tiq2Bw |access-date=2 April 2023 |work=www.ntv.com.tr |date=2 April 2023 |language=tr}} Recent attacks on other parties have raised issues of political polarisation and security in the country.{{Cite web |date=21 April 2023 |title=Armed attack on AKP office in Adana |url=https://m.bianet.org/english/politics/277621-armed-attack-on-akp-office-in-adana |website=Bianet |access-date=1 May 2023 |archive-date=23 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230423235433/https://m.bianet.org/english/politics/277621-armed-attack-on-akp-office-in-adana |url-status=live }} On 1 May, a group of unidentified individuals armed with guns and sticks assaulted [[Free Cause Party|HUDAPAR]] youth members in [[Mersin]]. HUDAPAR was hosting an election campaign stand to help their electoral ally the [[AK Party]]. {{Politics of South Africa}}

General elections were held in [[South Africa]] on 29 May 2024 to elect a new [[National Assembly (South Africa)|National Assembly]] as well as the [[Provincial legislature (South Africa)|provincial legislature]] in each of the [[Provinces of South Africa|nine provinces]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=20 February 2024 |title=South Africa to hold general election on May 29 |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/2/20/south-africa-to-hold-general-election-on-may-29 |access-date=29 February 2024 |website=[[Al Jazeera]]|archive-date=19 April 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240419095009/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/2/20/south-africa-to-hold-general-election-on-may-29 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=21 February 2024 |title=South Africa to hold elections on May 29 |url=https://www.aa.com.tr/en/africa/south-africa-to-hold-elections-on-may-29/3143370 |access-date=29 February 2024 |website=[[Aa.com.tr]] |archive-date=29 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240229220347/https://www.aa.com.tr/en/africa/south-africa-to-hold-elections-on-may-29/3143370 |url-status=live }}</ref> This was the seventh general election held under the conditions of [[universal adult suffrage]] since the end of the [[apartheid]] era in 1994. The [[National Council of Provinces]] (NCOP), the upper house of the [[Parliament of South Africa]], was elected by the provincial legislatures on 13 and 14 June after the general election.

Support for the ruling [[African National Congress]] (ANC) significantly declined in this election; the ANC remained the largest party but lost the parliamentary majority that it had held since the [[1994 South African general election|inaugural post-apartheid election in 1994]]. The [[Democratic Alliance (South Africa)|Democratic Alliance]] (DA) remained in second place with a slight increase. [[UMkhonto we Sizwe (political party)|uMkhonto we Sizwe]] (MK), a [[left-wing populist]] party founded 6 months prior to the election and led by former president [[Jacob Zuma]], came in third place.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.enca.com/news-top-stories/2024-elections-enca-projects-anc-will-take-45-national-vote|title=2024 ELECTIONS: eNCA Project ANC Will Take 45% Of National Vote|publisher=eNCA|date=30 May 2024|accessdate=30 May 2024|archive-date=30 May 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240530123735/https://www.enca.com/news-top-stories/2024-elections-enca-projects-anc-will-take-45-national-vote|url-status=live}}</ref> Several smaller parties received too few votes in the regional constituencies to secure a seat but received enough votes overall to win seats in the National Assembly (based on their allocation of compensatory seats).<ref>Electoral Reform Consultation Panel Original Report, pg. 45 https://www.dha.gov.za/images/ecrp/ERCP_Original_Report.pdf</ref>

On 14 June 2024, the ANC, the DA, the [[Inkatha Freedom Party]] (IFP) and the [[Patriotic Alliance]] (PA), agreed to form a national unity government, with [[Cyril Ramaphosa]] being re-elected [[President of South Africa]].<ref name=ancda>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c8007w4vqveo|title=ANC and DA agree on South Africa unity government|first1=Farouk|last1=Chothia|first2=Danai Kesta|last2=Kupemba|first3=Barbra|last3=Plett-Usher|publisher=BBC News|date=14 June 2024|accessdate=14 June 2024|archive-date=14 June 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240614112052/https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c8007w4vqveo|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=ramaphosare-elected>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/south-africas-national-assembly-re-elects-cyril-ramaphosa-president-2024-06-14/|title=South Africa's National Assembly re-elects Cyril Ramaphosa as president|publisher=Reuters|date=14 June 2024|accessdate=14 June 2024}}</ref>

== Background ==
The election date of 29 May 2024 was declared by the incumbent president [[Cyril Ramaphosa]] on 20 February.<ref>{{Cite news |date=24 October 2023 |title=Election season kicks off but no date yet |url=https://www.businesslive.co.za/bd/national/2023-10-24-election-season-kicks-off-but-no-date-yet/ |work=[[Business Day (South Africa)|Business Day]] |access-date=29 December 2023 |archive-date=29 December 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231229182105/https://www.businesslive.co.za/bd/national/2023-10-24-election-season-kicks-off-but-no-date-yet/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=20 February 2024 |title=President Cyril Ramaphosa announces 2024 General Elections date |url=https://www.gov.za/news/media-statements/president-cyril-ramaphosa-announces-2024-general-elections-date-20-feb-2024 |publisher=[[South African Government]] |access-date=20 February 2024 |archive-date=20 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240220174859/https://www.gov.za/news/media-statements/president-cyril-ramaphosa-announces-2024-general-elections-date-20-feb-2024 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Going into the election, polls showed that support for the ANC was declining significantly, leading to expectations of a [[hung parliament]].<ref>{{Cite news |title=Support for ANC will continue to decline following South Africa elections, pollster predicts |url=https://www.irishtimes.com/world/africa/2024/01/23/support-for-anc-will-continue-to-decline-following-south-africa-elections-pollster-predicts/ |access-date=31 January 2024 |newspaper=The Irish Times|archive-date=31 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240131225830/https://www.irishtimes.com/world/africa/2024/01/23/support-for-anc-will-continue-to-decline-following-south-africa-elections-pollster-predicts/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In the [[2021 South African municipal elections]], the [[African National Congress]] received less than 50% of the total vote for the first time since the end of apartheid,<ref>{{Cite web |date=5 November 2021 |title=A landmark as South Africa's ANC dips below 50% support |url=https://apnews.com/article/africa-elections-cape-town-race-and-ethnicity-racial-injustice-5d14a119310380ca61ce9eb7c3d3d6c2 |access-date=1 August 2023 |website=AP News|archive-date=1 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230801181437/https://apnews.com/article/africa-elections-cape-town-race-and-ethnicity-racial-injustice-5d14a119310380ca61ce9eb7c3d3d6c2 |url-status=live }}</ref> also losing support in the key metros of [[City of Tshwane Metropolitan Municipality|Tshwane]] (Pretoria), [[City of Johannesburg Metropolitan Municipality|Johannesburg]], [[City of Ekurhuleni Metropolitan Municipality|Ekurhuleni]], and [[EThekwini Metropolitan Municipality|eThekwini]] (Durban). The ANC retained control of eThekwini while the [[Democratic Alliance (South Africa)|Democratic Alliance]] managed to take control of Johannesburg and Ekurhuleni through a majority coalition and a minority coalition respectively, in addition to forming a majority coalition government in Tshwane, which it had governed since 2016.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Harper |first=Paddy |title=Historic losses for ANC open new era in South African politics |url=https://www.africanews.com/2021/11/06/historic-losses-for-anc-open-new-era-in-south-african-politics/ |access-date=1 August 2023 |work=Africanews|archive-date=1 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230801181438/https://www.africanews.com/2021/11/06/historic-losses-for-anc-open-new-era-in-south-african-politics/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In early 2023, the ANC and [[Economic Freedom Fighters]] formed a coalition in [[City of Johannesburg Metropolitan Municipality|Johannesburg]] and [[City of Ekurhuleni Metropolitan Municipality|Ekurhuleni]] where the two parties held MMC positions whilst electing a mayor from a minority party.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ANC and EFF partnership 'negotiating in good faith' to govern Gauteng metros |url=https://www.702.co.za/articles/466111/anc-and-eff-partnership-negotiating-in-good-faith-to-govern-gauteng-metros |access-date=1 August 2023 |website=702|archive-date=1 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230801181438/https://www.702.co.za/articles/466111/anc-and-eff-partnership-negotiating-in-good-faith-to-govern-gauteng-metros |url-status=live }}</ref> In April 2023, noting the prospects of an ANC/EFF national coalition, the DA leader [[John Steenhuisen]] called for "like-minded" parties to join to prevent a "doomsday coalition".<ref>{{Cite web |title=DA to fight ANC-EFF 'doomsday coalition' |url=https://www.businesslive.co.za/bd/politics/2023-04-02-da-to-fight-anc-eff-doomsday-coalition/ |url-access=subscription |access-date=1 August 2023 |website=BusinessLIVE|date=2 April 2023 |archive-date=1 August 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230801181437/https://www.businesslive.co.za/bd/politics/2023-04-02-da-to-fight-anc-eff-doomsday-coalition/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

===uMkhonto we Sizwe===
On 16 December 2023, former president [[Jacob Zuma]] announced his departure from the ANC, accusing the party and incumbent president [[Cyril Ramaphosa]] of serving as a "proxy for white monopoly capital." He was also noted as calling the ANC "sellouts" and "[[apartheid]] collaborators". === Voter turnout ===
Voter turnout has declined since the [[Negotiations to end apartheid in South Africa|end of apartheid]], when 86% of eligible voters turned out.<ref>{{Cite news |title=South Africa faces a defining election |url=https://www.economist.com/the-world-ahead/2023/11/13/south-africa-faces-a-defining-election |access-date=31 January 2024 |newspaper=The Economist |issn=0013-0613 |archive-date=31 January 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240131225831/https://www.economist.com/the-world-ahead/2023/11/13/south-africa-faces-a-defining-election |url-status=live }}</ref> For this election, 27 million people were eligible to vote.<ref name="logistics" /> Fifty-five percent of them were women, while voter registration was highest among those aged between 30 and 39 years old.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Counting under way in South Africa's crucial election |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cjll8nr6962o |access-date=30 May 2024 |publisher=BBC |archive-date=30 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240530005713/https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cjll8nr6962o |url-status=live }}</ref> Only 58% of the country's registered voters voted in the election.

==Electoral system==
South Africa has a [[Parliamentary system|parliamentary system of government]]. The [[president of South Africa]] is unusual among [[Head of state|heads of state]] of countries with a parliamentary system in that the [[head of government]], who holds executive powers, is titled president and also plays the ceremonial role of [[head of state]].

In June 2020, the [[Constitutional Court of South Africa|Constitutional Court]] ruled in ''[[New Nation Movement NPC v President of the Republic of South Africa]]'' that the [[Electoral Act, 1998|Electoral Act]] was unconstitutional to the extent that it did not allow independents to contest national and provincial elections.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Mabuza |first=Ernest |date=11 June 2020 |title=Constitutional Court judgment opens door for independent candidates to stand for election |url=https://www.timeslive.co.za/politics/2020-06-11-concourt-ruling-opens-door-for-independent-candidates-to-stand-for-election-in-sa/ |access-date=7 July 2021 |work=[[Sunday Times (South Africa)|Sunday Times]]|archive-date=9 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210709183738/https://www.timeslive.co.za/politics/2020-06-11-concourt-ruling-opens-door-for-independent-candidates-to-stand-for-election-in-sa/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Since the first elections held under [[universal suffrage]], 400 members elected were elected to the National Assembly by a system of [[proportional representation]] with a [[closed list]] approach. Two hundred members were elected from national party lists, while the other 200 were elected from provincial party lists in each of the [[Provinces of South Africa|nine provinces]]. The national list seats were awarded by subtracting seats won at the provincial level from each party's national allocation to generate a maximally proportional result. The [[Droop quota]] variant of the [[largest remainder method]] was used to allocate seats at both the national and provincial levels.<ref name="electionguide">{{Cite web |title=Election for National Assembly |url=http://www.electionguide.org/elections/id/2721/ |access-date=4 January 2020 |website=IFES Election Guide |archive-date=29 December 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141229211847/http://www.electionguide.org/elections/id/2721/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Provincial legislatures were also elected by a system of proportional representation with closed party lists.

In February 2021, [[Minister of Home Affairs (South Africa)|home affairs minister]] [[Aaron Motsoaledi]] appointed a ministerial advisory committee led by [[Valli Moosa]] to recommend a new electoral system.<ref>{{Cite web |date=24 March 2021 |title=Ministerial Advisory Committee on the Electoral System hosts first consultative meeting |url=https://www.gov.za/speeches/ministerial-advisory-committee-electoral-system-hosts-first-consultative-meeting-24-mar |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210709183523/https://www.gov.za/speeches/ministerial-advisory-committee-electoral-system-hosts-first-consultative-meeting-24-mar |archive-date=9 July 2021 |access-date=7 July 2021 |website=gov.za |publisher=[[Government of South Africa]]}}</ref> While the committee was divided in opinion, a slim majority of members favoured a [[mixed-member proportional]] system, with half of the seats elected in single-member [[Electoral district|constituencies]] and the other half elected from [[Party-list proportional representation|party lists]] in one national multi-member constituency.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Kgosana |first1=Caiphus |last2=Khoza |first2=Amanda |date=13 June 2021 |title=Advisory committee divided on which electoral system to adopt |url=https://www.timeslive.co.za/sunday-times/news/2021-06-13-advisory-committee-divided-on-which-electoral-system-to-adopt/ |access-date=7 July 2021 |work=[[Sunday Times (South Africa)|Sunday Times]]|archive-date=6 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210706220231/https://www.timeslive.co.za/sunday-times/news/2021-06-13-advisory-committee-divided-on-which-electoral-system-to-adopt/ |url-status=live }}{{subscription required|s}}</ref> Due to dissatisfaction with the process surrounding the adoption of the Electoral Amendment Bill, a review clause was inserted into the Bill providing for the establishment of the [[Electoral Reform Consultation Panel]]. In August 2025, the [[Electoral Reform Consultation Panel]] issued its final report recommending reducing the size of constituencies to bring representatives closer to voters.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Electoral Reform Consultation Panel |title=Electoral Reform Consultation Panel Final Report |url=https://static.pmg.org.za/ERCP_Original_Report.pdf}}</ref> 

=== Regional ballot ===
The regional ballot is one of the two ballots used in South Africa's national elections, alongside the national ballot. Voters were also presented with a third ballot, a single ballot used for the election of members of the nine provincial legislatures, held on the same day. The regional ballot is used to elect representatives to the National Assembly from each of the country's nine provinces. The regional ballot is proportional, meaning that seats are allocated to parties and independent candidates based on the number of votes received.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2024 General Elections, 29 May |url=https://www.gov.za/news/elections2024 |access-date=13 May 2024 |website=gov.za |archive-date=13 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240513205340/https://www.gov.za/news/elections2024 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Election of the National Assembly and provincial legislatures ===
On 17 April 2023, president [[Cyril Ramaphosa]] signed the [[South African Electoral Amendment Bill]] into law allowing independent candidates to stand for election to the National Assembly and provincial legislatures while keeping proportional representation with closed lists. Two hundred members will be elected from national party lists, while the remaining 200 seats will be contested by political parties and independent candidates in each of the nine provinces. In provincial legislatures, the single-tier multimember proportional system will continue to apply, with political parties and independent candidates contesting for seats. Voters will receive three ballot papers as opposed to two in previous elections; the first ballot will be to elect the 200 members of the National Assembly only contested by political parties; the second ballot will be to elect the remaining 200 members of the National Assembly, which will be contested by political parties and independent candidates in each of the nine provinces; and the third ballot will be to elect members of the provincial legislatures with political parties and independent candidates as well.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What's new in the 2024 Elections? |url=https://www.elections.org.za/pw/elections/whats-new-in-the-2024-elections-electoral-amendment-act |access-date=18 October 2023 |website=Electoral Commission of South Africa |archive-date=19 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231019153453/https://www.elections.org.za/pw/elections/whats-new-in-the-2024-elections-electoral-amendment-act |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Election of the president and premiers ===
Following the election, the [[president of South Africa]] was elected by the National Assembly. Although the president is required to be a member of the National Assembly at the time of election, a person who is elected as president must resign their seat in order to assume office.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Paton |first1=Carol |last2=Quintal |first2=Genevieve |date=22 May 2019 |title=Cyril Ramaphosa elected as president by National Assembly |url=https://www.businesslive.co.za/bd/national/2019-05-22-cyril-ramaphosa-elected-as-president-by-national-assembly/ |access-date=4 January 2020 |work=BusinessDay |archive-date=4 June 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190604173028/https://www.businesslive.co.za/bd/national/2019-05-22-cyril-ramaphosa-elected-as-president-by-national-assembly/ |url-status=live }}{{subscription required|s}}</ref> The premiers of each province will also be elected by the respective provincial legislatures after the election.<ref name="electionguide" />

=== NCOP elections ===
The [[National Council of Provinces]] (NCOP) comprises 90 members, ten of whom are elected by each of the provincial legislatures in proportion to the composition of the legislature. The NCOP members will be sworn in the day after the first sitting of the National Assembly.<ref name="electionguide" />

==Campaign issues==
=== Healthcare ===
On 15 May 2024, two weeks before the election, president Ramaphosa signed the National Health Insurance (NHI) Act into law, establishing a [[National Health Insurance (South Africa)|National Health Insurance]] state fund to provide more South Africans access to private healthcare.<ref>{{Cite web |date=15 May 2024 |title=A new South Africa health law aims at deep inequality, but critics say they'll challenge it |url=https://apnews.com/article/south-africa-health-law-elections-e1e15892eaa6efa51cc1bf14959d3453 |access-date=19 May 2024 |website=AP News|archive-date=19 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240519030656/https://apnews.com/article/south-africa-health-law-elections-e1e15892eaa6efa51cc1bf14959d3453 |url-status=live }}</ref> The goal of the bill is to eventually phase out the use of private healthcare, replacing it with the NHI as the sole purchaser and provider of health insurance. The DA is staunchly opposed to the bill on the premise that it could lead to large tax increases and corruption by ANC "[[cadre deployment]]," and have promised to challenge it in court.<ref name="BBC100">{{Cite web |title=South Africa's National Health Insurance (NHI) Bill: Why it is controversial |date=15 May 2024 |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c1030v3p1r8o |access-date=19 May 2024 |publisher=BBC|archive-date=19 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240519030656/https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c1030v3p1r8o |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Al10">{{Cite web |title=South Africa's Ramaphosa signs health bill weeks before election |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/5/15/south-africas-ramaphosa-signs-health-bill-weeks-before-election |access-date=19 May 2024 |website=Al Jazeera|archive-date=19 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240519031139/https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2024/5/15/south-africas-ramaphosa-signs-health-bill-weeks-before-election |url-status=live }}</ref>

The bill has been controversial because it would limit the ability for people to take out private health insurance to cover medical costs. Additionally, the government has not released official statistics regarding how much the NHI program would cost, raising concerns it could exacerbate South Africa's ongoing troubles providing public services such as [[South African energy crisis|electricity]] and water.<ref>[https://www.npr.org/2024/04/01/1241232636/johannesburg-south-africa-water-crisis Johannesburg's water crisis is the latest blow to South Africa's 'world-class city'] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240519030657/https://www.npr.org/2024/04/01/1241232636/johannesburg-south-africa-water-crisis |date=19 May 2024 }}. April 1, 2024. [[National Public Radio|NPR]]. Kate Bartlett.</ref><ref name=BBC100/><ref name=Al10/>

=== Corruption ===
{{Main|Corruption in South Africa|The Judicial Commission of Inquiry into Allegations of State Capture}}

[[The Judicial Commission of Inquiry into Allegations of State Capture]], known colloquially as the Zondo Commission, completed its work and submitted its final report to the president in June 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Zondo Commission: A bite-sized summary |url=https://pari.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/PARI-Summary-The-Zondo-Commission-A-bite-sized-summary-v360.pdf |access-date=5 March 2024 |website=Public Affairs Research Institute |archive-date=30 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231130095327/http://pari.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/PARI-Summary-The-Zondo-Commission-A-bite-sized-summary-v360.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> The Commission cost the South African taxpayer "almost R1 billion".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Haffajee |first=Ferial |date=30 June 2021 |title=State Capture Inquiry cost almost R1bn, but it saved billions more – Judge Zondo |url=https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2021-06-30-state-capture-inquiry-cost-almost-r1bn-but-it-saved-billions-more-judge-zondo/ |access-date=5 March 2024 |website=[[Daily Maverick]]|archive-date=1 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240601125242/https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2021-06-30-state-capture-inquiry-cost-almost-r1bn-but-it-saved-billions-more-judge-zondo/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Investigator Paul Holden of Shadow World Investigations read into evidence that [[state capture]] cost the South African economy at least R49 billion.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Davis |first=Rebecca |date=24 May 2021 |title=The total(ish) cost of the Guptas' State Capture: R49,157,323,233.68 |url=https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2021-05-24-the-totalish-cost-of-the-guptas-state-capture-r49157323233-68/ |access-date=5 March 2024 |website=[[Daily Maverick]]|archive-date=2 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240602154559/https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2021-05-24-the-totalish-cost-of-the-guptas-state-capture-r49157323233-68/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In their 2024 election manifesto, the [[African National Congress]] claims that, as per the Zondo Commission's recommendations, "laws, institutions and practices are being put in place to reduce the potential for corruption of any sort and on any scale".<ref>{{Cite web |title=The ANC's 2024 Manifesto – DOCUMENTS |url=https://www.politicsweb.co.za/documents/the-ancs-2024-manifesto |access-date=5 March 2024 |website=PoliticsWeb.co.za|archive-date=1 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240301032413/https://www.politicsweb.co.za/documents/the-ancs-2024-manifesto |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[Democratic Alliance (South Africa)|Democratic Alliance]] puts the blame for corruption and state capture squarely on the shoulders of the ANC, saying that it will "establish a genuinely independent anti-crime and anti-corruption unit by dissolving the [[Hawks (South Africa)|Hawks]] and establishing a new [[Chapter 9 institution]], an Anti-Corruption Commission, which will only be accountable to the [[Parliament of South Africa]]."<ref>{{Cite web |title=The DA's Rescue Plan for South Africa |url=https://cdn.da.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/16143750/DA-Election-Manifesto-2024.pdf |access-date=5 March 2024 |website=Democratic Alliance |archive-date=29 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240229172846/https://cdn.da.org.za/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/16143750/DA-Election-Manifesto-2024.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[Economic Freedom Fighters]] proposes to amend the [[Constitution of South Africa|Constitution]] to "make the [[National Prosecuting Authority]] a Chapter 9 institution accountable to Parliament".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Our Land & Jobs Now. Stop Loadshedding! 2024 Election Manifesto |url=https://effonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/A5-EFF-2024-Manifesto-full-version.pdf |access-date=5 March 2024 |website=Economic Freedom Fighters |archive-date=9 March 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240309185642/https://effonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/A5-EFF-2024-Manifesto-full-version.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

The ANC was also criticized for provisionally including four ministers ([[Zizi Kodwa]], [[Malusi Gigaba]], [[David Mahlobo]], and [[Gwede Mantashe]]) who were implicated in a corruption investigation into the administration of former president [[Jacob Zuma]] on 11 March, pending the final results of an intraparty review. Fourteen other officials were either disqualified or not listed as candidates by the ANC over the same issue.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Imray |first=Gerald |date=12 March 2024 |title=South Africa's ruling party fields election candidates who have faced graft allegations |url=https://apnews.com/article/south-africa-elections-anc-fa83145d9cd1080abde8fc4076817832 |access-date=12 March 2024 |work=Associated Press |archive-date=1 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240601125823/https://apnews.com/article/south-africa-elections-anc-fa83145d9cd1080abde8fc4076817832 |url-status=live }}</ref>
